It was created for use by [visual artists](/wiki/Artist "Artist") to put on their artwork to corrupt the data set of [text-to-image models](/wiki/Text-to-image_model "Text-to-image model"), which usually scrape their data from the internet without the consent of the image creator.[[29]](#cite_note-Edwards2023-29)[[30]](#cite_note-30)

[McAfee](/wiki/McAfee "McAfee") attacked [Tesla](/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. "Tesla, Inc.")'s former [Mobileye](/wiki/Mobileye "Mobileye") system, fooling it into driving 50 mph over the speed limit, simply by adding a two-inch strip of black tape to a speed limit sign.[[31]](#cite_note-31)[[32]](#cite_note-32)

Adversarial patterns on glasses or clothing designed to deceive facial-recognition systems or license-plate readers, have led to a niche industry of "stealth streetwear".[[33]](#cite_note-33)

An adversarial attack on a neural network can allow an attacker to inject algorithms into the target system.[[34]](#cite_note-nature_why2-34) Researchers can also create adversarial audio inputs to disguise commands to intelligent assistants in benign-seeming audio;[[35]](#cite_note-35) a parallel literature explores human perception of such stimuli.[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)

Clustering algorithms are used in security applications. Malware and [computer virus](/wiki/Computer_viruses "Computer viruses") analysis aims to identify malware families, and to generate specific detection signatures.[[38]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_42A2-38)[[39]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_46A2-39)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
Clustering algorithms are used in security applications. Malware and [computer virus](/wiki/Computer_viruses "Computer viruses") analysis aims to identify malware families, and to generate specific detection signatures.[[38]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_42A2-38)[[39]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_46A2-39)

In the context of malware detection, researchers have proposed methods for adversarial malware generation that automatically craft binaries to evade learning-based detectors while preserving malicious functionality. Optimization-based attacks such as GAMMA use genetic algorithms to inject benign content (for example, padding or new [PE](/wiki/Portable_Executable "Portable Executable") sections) into Windows executables, framing evasion as a constrained optimization problem that balances misclassification success with the size of the injected payload and showing transferability to commercial antivirus products.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Complementary work uses [generative adversarial networks](/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network") (GANs) to learn feature-space perturbations that cause malware to be classified as benign; Mal-LSGAN, for instance, replaces the standard GAN [loss](/wiki/Loss_function "Loss function") with a least-squares objective and modified [activation functions](/wiki/Activation_function "Activation function") to improve training stability and produce adversarial malware examples that substantially reduce true positive rates across multiple detectors.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
In the context of malware detection, researchers have proposed methods for adversarial malware generation that automatically craft binaries to evade learning-based detectors while preserving malicious functionality. Optimization-based attacks such as GAMMA use genetic algorithms to inject benign content (for example, padding or new [PE](/wiki/Portable_Executable "Portable Executable") sections) into Windows executables, framing evasion as a constrained optimization problem that balances misclassification success with the size of the injected payload and showing transferability to commercial antivirus products.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Complementary work uses [generative adversarial networks](/wiki/Generative_adversarial_network "Generative adversarial network") (GANs) to learn feature-space perturbations that cause malware to be classified as benign; Mal-LSGAN, for instance, replaces the standard GAN [loss](/wiki/Loss_function "Loss function") with a least-squares objective and modified [activation functions](/wiki/Activation_function "Activation function") to improve training stability and produce adversarial malware examples that substantially reduce true positive rates across multiple detectors.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

Emerging adversarial attacks are also highly effective in human-action recognition systems,[[42]](#cite_note-qiao25geometric-42) which are employed widely for real-world applications such as surveillance, autonomous vehicles, and in-house monitoring. In these attacks, attackers introduce noise into the representation of the human features to fool the recognition systems.[[43]](#cite_note-lu23hard-43) These attacks do not necessary require the access of the recognition systems themselves, and they can be inperceptible by the human users of such systems, thereby casting a significant security risk.[[44]](#cite_note-chang26quality-44)

title: Adversarial machine learning
section: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
## Challenges in applying machine learning to security

Researchers have observed that the constraints under which machine-learning techniques function in the security domain are different from those of common benchmark domains. Security data may change over time, include mislabeled samples, or reflect adversarial behavior, which complicates evaluation and reproducibility.[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Data collection issues

Security datasets vary across formats, including binaries, network traces, and log files. Studies have reported that the process of converting these sources into [features](/wiki/Feature_(machine_learning) "Feature (machine learning)") can introduce [bias](/wiki/Bias_(statistics) "Bias (statistics)") or inconsistencies.[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)
In addition, time-based [leakage](/wiki/Leakage_(machine_learning) "Leakage (machine learning)") can occur when related malware samples are not properly separated across [training](/wiki/Training_data_set "Training data set") and [testing](/wiki/Test_set "Test set") splits, which may lead to overly optimistic results.[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Labeling and ground truth challenges

Malware labels are often unstable because different antivirus engines may classify the same sample in conflicting ways. Ceschin et al. note that families may be renamed or reorganized over time, causing further discrepancies in [ground truth](/wiki/Ground_truth "Ground truth") and reducing the reliability of benchmarks.[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Concept drift

Because malware creators continuously adapt their techniques, the statistical properties of malicious samples also change. This form of [concept drift](/wiki/Concept_drift "Concept drift") has been widely documented and may reduce model performance unless systems are updated regularly or incorporate mechanisms for [incremental learning](/wiki/Incremental_learning "Incremental learning").[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Feature robustness

Researchers differentiate between features that can be easily manipulated and those that are more resistant to modification. For example, simple static attributes, such as header fields, may be altered by attackers, while structural features, such as [control-flow graphs](/wiki/Control-flow_graph "Control-flow graph"), are generally more stable but computationally expensive to [extract](/wiki/Feature_extraction "Feature extraction").[[45]](#cite_note-Ceschin2023-45)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Class imbalance

In realistic deployment environments, the proportion of malicious samples can be extremely low, ranging from 0.01% to 2% of total data. This unbalanced distribution causes models to develop a bias towards the majority class, achieving high accuracy but failing to identify malicious samples.[[46]](#cite_note-:16-46)

Prior approaches to this problem have included both data-level solutions and sequence-specific models. Methods like [n-gram](/wiki/N-gram "N-gram") and [Long Short-Term Memory](/wiki/Long_short-term_memory "Long short-term memory") (LSTM) networks can model sequential data, but their performance has been shown to decline significantly when malware samples are realistically proportioned in the training set, demonstrating the limitations in realistic security contexts.[[46]](#cite_note-:16-46)

To address this issue, one approach has been to adapt models from [natural language processing](/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing"), such as [BERT](/wiki/BERT_(language_model) "BERT (language model)"). This method involves treating sequences of application activities as a form of "language" and [fine-tuning](/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning) "Fine-tuning (deep learning)") a pre-trained BERT model on the specific task. A study applying this technique to Android activity sequences reported an [F1 score](/wiki/F1_score "F1 score") of 0.919 on a dataset with only 0.5% malware samples. This result was a significant improvement over LSTM and n-gram models, demonstrating the potential of pre-trained models to handle class imbalance in malware detection.[[46]](#cite_note-:16-46)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### System design and learning

[Feature engineering](/wiki/Feature_engineering "Feature engineering") and training can causes issues. [Data snooping](/wiki/Data_snooping "Data snooping") is a common pitfall where a model is trained using information that would not be available in a real-world scenario.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47) [Spurious correlations](/wiki/Spurious_correlation "Spurious correlation") result when a model learns to associate artifacts with a label, rather than the underlying security-relevant pattern.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47) For example, a malware classifier might learn to identify a specific compiler artifact instead of malicious behavior itself.
Biased parameter selection is a form of data snooping where model [hyperparameters](/wiki/Hyperparameter_(machine_learning) "Hyperparameter (machine learning)") are tuned using the [test set](/wiki/Test_set "Test set").[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Performance evaluation

The choice of the evaluation metrics can impact the validity of the results.
Having an inappropriate baseline involves failing to compare a new model against simpler, well-established baselines.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)
Inappropriate performance measures means using metrics that do not align with the practical goals of the system.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47) Reporting only "[accuracy](/wiki/Accuracy "Accuracy")" is often described as insufficient for an intrusion detection system, where [false-positive rates](/wiki/False_positive_rate "False positive rate") are considered critically important.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)
[Base rate fallacy](/wiki/Base_rate_fallacy "Base rate fallacy") is a failure to correctly interpret performance in the context of large class imbalances.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)

title: Adversarial machine learning
heading_path: Challenges in applying machine learning to security
text:
### Deployment and operation

Deployment introduces challenges related to the performance and security in live environments.
Lab-only evaluation is the practice of evaluating a system only in a controlled, static laboratory setting, which does not account for real-world challenges like concept drift and performance overhead.[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)
Inappropriate threat model refers to failing to consider the ML system itself as an [attack surface](/wiki/Attack_surface "Attack surface").[[47]](#cite_note-:15-47)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text: ## Attack modalities

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Taxonomy

Attacks against ([supervised](/wiki/Supervised_learning "Supervised learning")) machine learning algorithms have been categorized along three primary axes:[[48]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_22-48) influence on the classifier, the security violation and their specificity.

- Classifier influence: An attack can influence the classifier by disrupting the classification phase. This may be preceded by an exploration phase to identify vulnerabilities. The attacker's capabilities might be restricted by the presence of data manipulation constraints.[[49]](#cite_note-49)
- Security violation: An attack can supply malicious data that gets classified as legitimate. Malicious data supplied during training can cause legitimate data to be rejected after training.
- Specificity: A targeted attack attempts to allow a specific intrusion/disruption. Alternatively, an indiscriminate attack creates general mayhem.

This taxonomy has been extended into a more comprehensive threat model that allows explicit assumptions about the adversary's goal, knowledge of the attacked system, capability of manipulating the input data/system components, and on attack strategy.[[50]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_4A2-50)[[51]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_5A2-51) This taxonomy has further been extended to include dimensions for defense strategies against adversarial attacks.[[52]](#cite_note-52)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Strategies

Below are some of the most commonly encountered attack scenarios.

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
#### Data poisoning

Poisoning consists of contaminating the training dataset with data designed to increase errors in the output. Given that learning algorithms are shaped by their training datasets, poisoning can effectively reprogram algorithms with potentially malicious intent. Concerns have been raised especially for user-generated training data, e.g. for [content recommendation](/wiki/Recommender_system "Recommender system") or natural language models. The ubiquity of fake accounts offers many opportunities for poisoning. Facebook reportedly removes around 7 billion fake accounts per year.[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54) Poisoning has been reported as the leading concern for industrial applications.[[55]](#cite_note-:1-55)

On social medias, [disinformation campaigns](/wiki/Disinformation "Disinformation") attempt to bias recommendation and moderation algorithms, to push certain content over others.[*[further explanation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*]

A particular case of data poisoning is the [backdoor](/wiki/Backdoor_(computing) "Backdoor (computing)") attack,[[56]](#cite_note-56) which aims to teach a specific behavior for inputs with a given trigger, e.g. a small defect on images, sounds, videos or texts.

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_%28Nightshade%29.png/250px-AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_%28Nightshade%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_(Nightshade).png)

AI training data poisoning illustration, showing how models can learn to associate given terms with wrong concepts due to data poisoning[[57]](#cite_note-57)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_%28Nightshade%29.png/250px-AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_%28Nightshade%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:AI_training_data_poisoning_illustration_(Nightshade).png)

AI training data poisoning illustration, showing how models can learn to associate given terms with wrong concepts due to data poisoning[[57]](#cite_note-57)

For instance, [intrusion detection systems](/wiki/Intrusion_detection_system "Intrusion detection system") are often trained using collected data. An attacker may poison this data by injecting malicious samples during operation that subsequently disrupt retraining.[[50]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_4A2-50)[[51]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_5A2-51)[[48]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_22-48)[[58]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_15A2-58)[[59]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_29A2-59)

Data poisoning techniques can also be applied to [text-to-image models](/wiki/Text-to-image_model "Text-to-image model") to alter their output, which is used by artists to defend their copyrighted works or their artistic style against imitation.[[29]](#cite_note-Edwards2023-29)

Data poisoning can also happen unintentionally through [model collapse](/wiki/Model_collapse "Model collapse"), where models are trained on synthetic data.[[60]](#cite_note-60)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
#### Byzantine attacks

As machine learning is scaled, it often relies on multiple computing machines. In [federated learning](/wiki/Federated_learning "Federated learning"), for instance, edge devices collaborate with a central server, typically by sending gradients or model parameters. However, some of these devices may deviate from their expected behavior, e.g. to harm the central server's model[[61]](#cite_note-Baruch_2019-61) or to bias algorithms towards certain behaviors (e.g., amplifying the recommendation of disinformation content). On the other hand, if the training is performed on a single machine, then the model is very vulnerable to a failure of the machine, or an attack on the machine; the machine is a [single point of failure](/wiki/Single_point_of_failure "Single point of failure").[[62]](#cite_note-62) In fact, the machine owner may themselves insert provably undetectable [backdoors](/wiki/Backdoor_(computing) "Backdoor (computing)").[[63]](#cite_note-63)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
As machine learning is scaled, it often relies on multiple computing machines. In [federated learning](/wiki/Federated_learning "Federated learning"), for instance, edge devices collaborate with a central server, typically by sending gradients or model parameters. However, some of these devices may deviate from their expected behavior, e.g. to harm the central server's model[[61]](#cite_note-Baruch_2019-61) or to bias algorithms towards certain behaviors (e.g., amplifying the recommendation of disinformation content). On the other hand, if the training is performed on a single machine, then the model is very vulnerable to a failure of the machine, or an attack on the machine; the machine is a [single point of failure](/wiki/Single_point_of_failure "Single point of failure").[[62]](#cite_note-62) In fact, the machine owner may themselves insert provably undetectable [backdoors](/wiki/Backdoor_(computing) "Backdoor (computing)").[[63]](#cite_note-63)

The current leading solutions to make (distributed) learning algorithms provably resilient to a minority of malicious (a.k.a. [Byzantine](/wiki/Byzantine_fault "Byzantine fault")) participants are based on [robust](/wiki/Robust_parameter_estimation "Robust parameter estimation") gradient aggregation rules.[[64]](#cite_note-:14-64)[[65]](#cite_note-65)[[66]](#cite_note-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)[[69]](#cite_note-69) The robust aggregation rules do not always work especially when the data across participants has a non-iid distribution. Nevertheless, in the context of heterogeneous honest participants, such as users with different consumption habits for recommendation algorithms or writing styles for language models, there are provable impossibility theorems on what any robust learning algorithm can guarantee.[[4]](#cite_note-:13-4)[[70]](#cite_note-70)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
#### Evasion

Evasion attacks[[8]](#cite_note-Springer-8)[[50]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_4A2-50)[[51]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_5A2-51)[[71]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_36A2-71) consist of exploiting the imperfection of a trained model. For instance, spammers and hackers often attempt to evade detection by obfuscating the content of spam emails and [malware](/wiki/Malware "Malware"). Samples are modified to evade detection; that is, to be classified as legitimate. This does not involve influence over the training data. A clear example of evasion is [image-based spam](/wiki/Image_spam "Image spam") in which the spam content is embedded within an attached image to evade textual analysis by anti-spam filters. Another example of evasion is given by spoofing attacks against biometric verification systems.[[22]](#cite_note-RodriguesLing20092-22)

Evasion attacks can be generally split into two different categories: [black box attacks](/wiki/Black_box "Black box") and [white box attacks](/wiki/White_box_(software_engineering) "White box (software engineering)").[[16]](#cite_note-:3-16)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
#### Model extraction

Model extraction involves an adversary probing a black box machine learning system in order to extract the data it was trained on.[[72]](#cite_note-72)[[73]](#cite_note-:12-73) This can cause issues when either the training data or the model itself is sensitive and confidential. For example, model extraction could be used to extract a proprietary stock trading model which the adversary could then use for their own financial benefit.

In the extreme case, model extraction can lead to model stealing, which corresponds to extracting a sufficient amount of data from the model to enable the complete reconstruction of the model.

On the other hand, membership inference is a targeted model extraction attack, which infers the owner of a data point, often by leveraging the [overfitting](/wiki/Overfitting "Overfitting") resulting from poor machine learning practices.[[74]](#cite_note-:6-74) Concerningly, this is sometimes achievable even without knowledge or access to a target model's parameters, raising security concerns for models trained on sensitive data, including but not limited to medical records and/or personally identifiable information. With the emergence of [transfer learning](/wiki/Transfer_learning "Transfer learning") and public accessibility of many state of the art machine learning models, tech companies are increasingly drawn to create models based on public ones, giving attackers freely accessible information to the structure and type of model being used.[[74]](#cite_note-:6-74)

text:
### Adversarial attacks and training in linear models

There is a growing literature about adversarial attacks in [linear models](/wiki/Linear_model "Linear model"). Indeed, since the seminal work from Goodfellow at al.[[75]](#cite_note-GoodfellowShlensSzegedy2015-75) studying these models in linear models has been an important tool to understand how adversarial attacks affect machine learning models.
The analysis of these models is simplified because the computation of adversarial attacks can be simplified in [linear regression](/wiki/Linear_regression "Linear regression") and [classification](/wiki/Linear_classification "Linear classification") problems. Moreover, adversarial training is [convex](/wiki/Convex_optimization "Convex optimization") in this case.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

Linear models allow for analytical analysis while still reproducing phenomena observed in state-of-the-art models.
One prime example of that is how this model can be used to explain the trade-off between [robustness](/wiki/Robustness_(statistics) "Robustness (statistics)") and [accuracy](/wiki/Accuracy "Accuracy").[[77]](#cite_note-77)
Diverse work indeed provides analysis of adversarial attacks in linear models, including asymptotic analysis for classification [[78]](#cite_note-78) and for linear regression.[[79]](#cite_note-79)[[80]](#cite_note-80) And, finite-sample analysis based on [Rademacher complexity](/wiki/Rademacher_complexity "Rademacher complexity").[[81]](#cite_note-81)

A result from studying adversarial attacks in linear models is that it closely relates to [regularization](/wiki/Regularization_(mathematics) "Regularization (mathematics)").[[82]](#cite_note-82) Under certain conditions, it has been shown that

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Adversarial deep reinforcement learning

Adversarial [deep reinforcement learning](/wiki/Deep_reinforcement_learning "Deep reinforcement learning") is an active area of research in [reinforcement learning](/wiki/Reinforcement_learning "Reinforcement learning") focusing on vulnerabilities of learned policies. In this research area, some studies initially showed that reinforcement learning policies are susceptible to imperceptible adversarial manipulations.[[75]](#cite_note-GoodfellowShlensSzegedy2015-75)[[83]](#cite_note-83) While some methods have been proposed to overcome these susceptibilities, in the most recent studies it has been shown that these proposed solutions are far from providing an accurate representation of current vulnerabilities of deep reinforcement learning policies.[[84]](#cite_note-84)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Adversarial natural language processing

Adversarial attacks on [speech recognition](/wiki/Speech_recognition "Speech recognition") have been introduced for speech-to-text applications, in particular for Mozilla's implementation of DeepSpeech[[85]](#cite_note-85) and Google's Speech Commands model.[[86]](#cite_note-86) Various pre-processing techniques have been proposed to defend against such attacks [[87]](#cite_note-87), but these methods may not be resilient to attackers aware of those defenses.

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
## Specific attack types

There are a large variety of different adversarial attacks that can be used against machine learning systems. Many of these work on both [deep learning](/wiki/Deep_learning "Deep learning") systems as well as traditional machine learning models such as [SVMs](/wiki/Support_vector_machine "Support vector machine")[[7]](#cite_note-Poisoning_Attacks_against_Support_V-7) and [linear regression](/wiki/Linear_regression "Linear regression").[[88]](#cite_note-88) A high level sample of these attack types include:

- Adversarial examples[[89]](#cite_note-89)
- Trojan and backdoor attacks[[90]](#cite_note-90)
- Model inversion[[91]](#cite_note-91)
- Membership inference[[92]](#cite_note-92)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Adversarial examples

An adversarial example refers to specially crafted input that is designed to look "normal" to humans but causes misclassification to a machine learning model. Often, a form of specially designed "noise" is used to elicit the misclassifications. Below are some current techniques for generating adversarial examples in the literature (by no means an exhaustive list).

- Gradient-based evasion attack[[8]](#cite_note-Springer-8)
- Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM)[[93]](#cite_note-Explaining_and_Harnessing_Adversari2-93)
- Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)[[94]](#cite_note-94)
- Carlini and Wagner (C&W) attack[[95]](#cite_note-95)
- Adversarial patch attack[[96]](#cite_note-96)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
#### Black box attacks

[Black box](/wiki/Black_box "Black box") attacks in adversarial machine learning assume that the adversary can only get outputs for provided inputs and has no knowledge of the model structure or parameters.[[16]](#cite_note-:3-16)[[97]](#cite_note-97) In this case, the adversarial example is generated either using a model created from scratch, or without any model at all (excluding the ability to query the original model). In either case, the objective of these attacks is to create adversarial examples that are able to transfer to the black box model in question.[[98]](#cite_note-:4-98)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
##### Simple black-box adversarial attacks

*Simple black-box adversarial attacks* is a query-efficient way to attack black-box image classifiers.[[99]](#cite_note-99)

##### Square attack

Square attacks were introduced in 2020 as a black-box evasion adversarial attack technique based on querying classification scores without the need for gradient information.[[101]](#cite_note-:7-101) As a score based black box attack, this adversarial approach is able to query probability distributions across model output classes, but has no other access to the model itself. According to the paper's authors, the proposed Square Attack required fewer queries than when compared to state-of-the-art score-based black box attacks at the time.[[101]](#cite_note-:7-101)

The result in theory is an adversarial example that is highly confident in the incorrect class but is also very similar to the original image. To find such example, Square Attack utilizes the iterative [random search](/wiki/Random_search "Random search") technique to randomly perturb the image in hopes of improving the objective function. In each step, the algorithm perturbs only a small square section of pixels, hence the name Square Attack, which terminates as soon as an adversarial example is found in order to improve query efficiency. Finally, since the attack algorithm uses scores and not gradient information, the authors of the paper indicate that this approach is not affected by gradient masking, a common technique formerly used to prevent evasion attacks.[[101]](#cite_note-:7-101)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
##### HopSkipJump attack

This black box attack was also proposed as a query efficient attack, but one that relies solely on access to any input's predicted output class. In other words, the HopSkipJump attack does not require the ability to calculate gradients or access to score values like the Square Attack, and will require just the model's class prediction output (for any given input). The proposed attack is split into two different settings, targeted and untargeted, but both are built from the general idea of adding minimal perturbations that leads to a different model output. In the targeted setting, the goal is to cause the model to misclassify the perturbed image to a specific target label (that is not the original label). In the untargeted setting, the goal is to cause the model to misclassify the perturbed image to any label that is not the original label. The attack objectives for both are as follows where

#### White box attacks

[White box](/wiki/White_box_(software_engineering) "White box (software engineering)") attacks assumes that the adversary has access to model parameters on top of being able to get labels for provided inputs.[[98]](#cite_note-:4-98)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
##### Fast gradient sign method

One of the first proposed attacks for generating adversarial examples was proposed by Google researchers [Ian J. Goodfellow](/wiki/Ian_Goodfellow "Ian Goodfellow"), Jonathon Shlens, and Christian Szegedy.[[105]](#cite_note-:9-105) The attack was called fast gradient sign method (FGSM), and it consists of adding a linear amount of in-perceivable noise to the image and causing a model to incorrectly classify it. This noise is calculated by multiplying the sign of the gradient with respect to the image we want to perturb by a small constant epsilon. As epsilon increases, the model is more likely to be fooled, but the perturbations become easier to identify as well. Shown below is the equation to generate an adversarial example where

The Fast Gradient Sign Method was proposed as a fast way to generate adversarial examples to evade the model, based on the hypothesis that neural networks cannot resist even linear amounts of perturbation to the input.[[107]](#cite_note-:10-107)[[106]](#cite_note-:11-106)[[105]](#cite_note-:9-105) FGSM has shown to be effective in adversarial attacks for image classification and skeletal action recognition.[[108]](#cite_note-coronafigueroaa23unaligned-108)

## Defenses

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Proactive_arms_race.jpg/250px-Proactive_arms_race.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Proactive_arms_race.jpg)

Conceptual representation of the proactive arms race[[51]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_5A2-51)[[39]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_46A2-39)

Researchers have proposed a multi-step approach to protecting machine learning.[[10]](#cite_note-:02-10)

- Threat modeling – formalize the attackers goals and capabilities with respect to the target system.
- Attack simulation – formalize the optimization problem the attacker tries to solve according to possible attack strategies.
- Attack impact evaluation
- Countermeasure design
- Noise detection (for evasion-based attack)[[112]](#cite_note-112)
- Information laundering – Alter the information received by adversaries (for model stealing attacks)[[73]](#cite_note-:12-73)

title: Adversarial machine learning
text:
### Mechanisms

A number of defense mechanisms against evasion, poisoning, and privacy attacks have been proposed, including:

- Secure learning algorithms[[19]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_18A2-19)[[113]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_22A2-113)[[114]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_45A2-114)
- Byzantine-resilient algorithms[[64]](#cite_note-:14-64)[[4]](#cite_note-:13-4)
- Multiple classifier systems[[18]](#cite_note-BiggioFumera20102-18)[[115]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_10A2-115)
- AI-written algorithms.[[34]](#cite_note-nature_why2-34)
- AIs that explore the training environment; for example, in image recognition, actively navigating a 3D environment rather than passively scanning a fixed set of 2D images.[[34]](#cite_note-nature_why2-34)
- Privacy-preserving learning[[51]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_5A2-51)[[116]](#cite_note-Adversarial_Machine_Learning_41A2-116)
- Ladder algorithm for [Kaggle](/wiki/Kaggle "Kaggle")-style competitions[[117]](#cite_note-117)
- Game theoretic models[[118]](#cite_note-feature_select2-118)[[119]](#cite_note-119)[[120]](#cite_note-120)
- Sanitizing training data
- Adversarial training[[93]](#cite_note-Explaining_and_Harnessing_Adversari2-93)[[21]](#cite_note-:0-21)
- Backdoor detection algorithms[[121]](#cite_note-121)
- Gradient masking/obfuscation techniques: to prevent the adversary exploiting the gradient in white-box attacks. This family of defenses is deemed unreliable as these models are still vulnerable to black-box attacks or can be circumvented in other ways.[[122]](#cite_note-122)
- [Ensembles](/wiki/Ensemble_learning "Ensemble learning") of models have been proposed in literature, which have shown to be ineffective against evasion attacks[[123]](#cite_note-123) but effective against data poisoning attacks.[[124]](#cite_note-124)
- Moving target defense[[125]](#cite_note-125)

title: Algorithm selection
text:
Meta-algorithmic technique to choose an algorithm

**Algorithm selection** (sometimes also called **per-instance algorithm selection** or **offline algorithm selection**) is a meta-[algorithmic technique](/wiki/Algorithmic_technique "Algorithmic technique") to choose an algorithm from a portfolio on an instance-by-instance basis. It is motivated by the observation that on many practical problems, different algorithms have different performance characteristics. That is, while one algorithm performs well in some scenarios, it performs poorly in others and vice versa for another algorithm. If we can identify when to use which algorithm, we can optimize for each scenario and improve overall performance. This is what algorithm selection aims to do. The only prerequisite for applying algorithm selection techniques is that there exists (or that there can be constructed) a set of complementary algorithms.

title: Algorithm selection
section: Boolean satisfiability problem (and other hard combinatorial problems)
heading_path: Boolean satisfiability problem (and other hard combinatorial problems)
text:
### Boolean satisfiability problem (and other hard combinatorial problems)

A well-known application of algorithm selection is the [Boolean satisfiability problem](/wiki/Boolean_satisfiability_problem "Boolean satisfiability problem"). Here, the portfolio of algorithms is a set of (complementary) [SAT solvers](/wiki/SAT_solver "SAT solver"), the instances are Boolean formulas, the cost metric is for example average runtime or number of unsolved instances. So, the goal is to select a well-performing SAT solver for each individual instance. In the same way, algorithm selection can be applied to many other

N
P
{\displaystyle {\mathcal {NP}}}
![{\displaystyle {\mathcal {NP}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/87fa655c6095197732cf6223a7749d794e08697d)-hard problems (such as [mixed integer programming](/wiki/Linear_programming "Linear programming"), [CSP](/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem "Constraint satisfaction problem"), [AI planning](/wiki/Automated_planning_and_scheduling "Automated planning and scheduling"), [TSP](/wiki/Travelling_salesman_problem "Travelling salesman problem"), [MAXSAT](/wiki/MAXSAT "MAXSAT"), [QBF](/wiki/QBF "QBF") and [answer set programming](/wiki/Answer_set_programming "Answer set programming")). Competition-winning systems in SAT are SATzilla,[[3]](#cite_note-zilla08-3) 3S[[4]](#cite_note-4) and CSHC[[5]](#cite_note-CSHC-5)

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Machine learning

In [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"), algorithm selection is better known as [meta-learning](/wiki/Meta-learning_(computer_science) "Meta-learning (computer science)"). The portfolio of algorithms consists of machine learning algorithms (e.g., [Random Forest](/wiki/Random_forest "Random forest"), SVM, DNN), the instances are [data sets](/wiki/Data_set "Data set") and the cost metric is for example the error rate. So, the goal is to predict which machine learning algorithm will have a small error on each data set.

title: Algorithm selection

The algorithm selection problem is mainly solved with machine learning techniques. By representing the problem instances by numerical features

f

Instance features are numerical representations of instances. For example, we can count the number of variables, clauses, average clause length for Boolean formulas,[[6]](#cite_note-6) or number of samples, features, class balance for ML data sets to get an impression about their characteristics.

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Static vs. probing features

We distinguish between two kinds of features:

1. Static features are in most cases some counts and statistics (e.g., clauses-to-variables ratio in SAT). These features ranges from very cheap features (e.g. number of variables) to very complex features (e.g., statistics about variable-clause graphs).
2. Probing features (sometimes also called landmarking features) are computed by running some analysis of algorithm behavior on an instance (e.g., accuracy of a cheap decision tree algorithm on an ML data set, or running for a short time a stochastic local search solver on a Boolean formula). These feature often cost more than simple static features.

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Feature costs

Depending on the used performance metric

m
{\displaystyle m}
![{\displaystyle m}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0a07d98bb302f3856cbabc47b2b9016692e3f7bc), feature computation can be associated with costs.
For example, if we use running time as performance metric, we include the time to compute our instance features into the performance of an algorithm selection system.
SAT solving is a concrete example, where such feature costs cannot be neglected, since instance features for [CNF](/wiki/Conjunctive_normal_form "Conjunctive normal form") formulas can be either very cheap (e.g., to get the number of variables can be done in constant time for CNFs in the [DIMACs](/wiki/DIMACS "DIMACS") format) or very expensive (e.g., graph features which can cost tens or hundreds of seconds).

It is important to take the overhead of feature computation into account in practice in such scenarios; otherwise a misleading impression of the performance of the algorithm selection approach is created. For example, if the decision which algorithm to choose can be made with perfect accuracy, but the features are the running time of the portfolio algorithms, there is no benefit to the portfolio approach. This would not be obvious if feature costs were omitted.

text:
### Clustering approach

A common assumption is that the given set of instances

I
{\displaystyle {\mathcal {I}}}

So, the training consists of identifying the homogeneous clusters via an unsupervised clustering approach and associating an algorithm with each cluster.
A new instance is assigned to a cluster and the associated algorithm selected.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

A more modern approach is cost-sensitive [hierarchical clustering](/wiki/Hierarchical_clustering "Hierarchical clustering")[[5]](#cite_note-CSHC-5) using [supervised learning](/wiki/Supervised_learning "Supervised learning") to identify the homogeneous instance subsets.

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Pairwise cost-sensitive classification approach

A common approach for multi-class classification is to learn pairwise models between every pair of classes (here algorithms)
and choose the class that was predicted most often by the pairwise models.
We can weight the instances of the pairwise prediction problem by the performance difference between the two algorithms.
This is motivated by the fact that we care most about getting predictions with large differences correct, but the penalty for an incorrect prediction is small if there is almost no performance difference.

text: - In some application, the computation of instance features is associated with a cost. For example, if the cost metric is running time, we have also to consider the time to compute the instance features. In such cases, the cost to compute features should not be larger than the performance gain through algorithm selection.

title: Algorithm selection
text:
## Application domains

Algorithm selection is not limited to single domains but can be applied to any kind of algorithm if the above requirements are satisfied.
Application domains include:

- hard combinatorial problems:[[10]](#cite_note-10) [SAT](/wiki/Boolean_satisfiability_problem "Boolean satisfiability problem"), [Mixed Integer Programming](/wiki/Linear_programming "Linear programming"), [CSP](/wiki/Constraint_satisfaction_problem "Constraint satisfaction problem"), [AI Planning](/wiki/Automated_planning_and_scheduling "Automated planning and scheduling"), [TSP](/wiki/Travelling_salesman_problem "Travelling salesman problem"), [MAXSAT](/wiki/MAXSAT "MAXSAT"), [QBF](/wiki/QBF "QBF") and [Answer Set Programming](/wiki/Answer_Set_Programming "Answer Set Programming")
- combinatorial auctions
- in machine learning, the problem is known as [meta-learning](/wiki/Meta-learning_(computer_science) "Meta-learning (computer science)")
- software design
- black-box optimization
- [multi-agent systems](/wiki/Multi-agent_system "Multi-agent system")
- numerical optimization
- [linear algebra](/wiki/Linear_algebra "Linear algebra"), differential equations
- [evolutionary algorithms](/wiki/Evolutionary_algorithm "Evolutionary algorithm")
- [vehicle routing problem](/wiki/Vehicle_routing_problem "Vehicle routing problem")
- power systems

For an extensive list of literature about algorithm selection, we refer to a literature overview.

title: Algorithm selection
text: ## Variants of algorithm selection

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Online selection

[Online algorithm](/wiki/Online_algorithm "Online algorithm") selection refers to switching between different algorithms during the solving process. This is useful as a [hyper-heuristic](/wiki/Hyper-heuristic "Hyper-heuristic"). In contrast, offline algorithm selection selects an algorithm for a given instance only once and before the solving process.

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Computation of schedules

An extension of algorithm selection is the per-instance algorithm scheduling problem, in which we do not select only one solver, but we select a time budget for each algorithm on a per-instance base. This approach improves the performance of selection systems in particular if the instance features are not very informative and a wrong selection of a single solver is likely.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

title: Algorithm selection
text:
### Selection of parallel portfolios

Given the increasing importance of parallel computation,
an extension of algorithm selection for parallel computation is parallel portfolio selection,
in which we select a subset of the algorithms to simultaneously run in a parallel portfolio.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

The following [outline](/wiki/Outline_(list) "Outline (list)") is provided as an overview of, and topical guide to, machine learning:

**Machine learning** (**ML**) is a subfield of [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") within [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science") that evolved from the study of [pattern recognition](/wiki/Pattern_recognition "Pattern recognition") and [computational learning theory](/wiki/Computational_learning_theory "Computational learning theory").[[1]](#cite_note-Britannica-1) In 1959, [Arthur Samuel](/wiki/Arthur_Samuel_(computer_scientist) "Arthur Samuel (computer scientist)") defined machine learning as a "field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed".[[2]](#cite_note-arthur_samuel_machine_learning_def-2) ML involves the study and construction of [algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm") that can [learn](/wiki/Learning "Learning") from and make predictions on [data](/wiki/Data "Data").[[3]](#cite_note-3) These algorithms operate by building a [model](/wiki/Mathematical_model "Mathematical model") from a [training set](/wiki/Training,_validation,_and_test_data_sets "Training, validation, and test data sets") of example observations to make data-driven predictions or decisions expressed as outputs, rather than following strictly static program instructions.

**Algorithmic bias** describes systematic and repeatable harmful tendency in a [computerized](/wiki/Computer_System "Computer System") [sociotechnical](/wiki/Sociotechnical_system "Sociotechnical system") system to create "[unfair](#Defining_fairness)" outcomes, such as "privileging" one category over another in ways that may or may not be different from the intended function of the algorithm.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
**Algorithmic bias** describes systematic and repeatable harmful tendency in a [computerized](/wiki/Computer_System "Computer System") [sociotechnical](/wiki/Sociotechnical_system "Sociotechnical system") system to create "[unfair](#Defining_fairness)" outcomes, such as "privileging" one category over another in ways that may or may not be different from the intended function of the algorithm.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Bias can emerge from many factors, including intentionally biased design decisions or the unintended or unanticipated use or decisions relating to the way data is coded, collected, selected or used to train the algorithm.[[3]](#cite_note-3) For example, algorithmic bias has been observed in [search engine results](/wiki/Search_engine_bias "Search engine bias") and [social media platforms](/wiki/Social_media_bias "Social media bias"). This bias can have impacts ranging from privacy violations to reinforcing [social biases](/wiki/Bias "Bias") of race, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity. The study of algorithmic bias is most concerned with algorithms that reflect "systematic and unfair" discrimination.[[4]](#cite_note-4) This bias has only recently been addressed in legal frameworks, such as the European Union's [General Data Protection Regulation](/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation "General Data Protection Regulation") (enforced in 2018) and the [Artificial Intelligence Act](/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Act "Artificial Intelligence Act") (proposed in 2021 and adopted in 2024).

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
Bias can emerge from many factors, including intentionally biased design decisions or the unintended or unanticipated use or decisions relating to the way data is coded, collected, selected or used to train the algorithm.[[3]](#cite_note-3) For example, algorithmic bias has been observed in [search engine results](/wiki/Search_engine_bias "Search engine bias") and [social media platforms](/wiki/Social_media_bias "Social media bias"). This bias can have impacts ranging from privacy violations to reinforcing [social biases](/wiki/Bias "Bias") of race, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity. The study of algorithmic bias is most concerned with algorithms that reflect "systematic and unfair" discrimination.[[4]](#cite_note-4) This bias has only recently been addressed in legal frameworks, such as the European Union's [General Data Protection Regulation](/wiki/General_Data_Protection_Regulation "General Data Protection Regulation") (enforced in 2018) and the [Artificial Intelligence Act](/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Act "Artificial Intelligence Act") (proposed in 2021 and adopted in 2024).

As algorithms expand their ability to organize society, politics, institutions, and behavior, sociologists have become concerned with the ways in which unanticipated output and manipulation of data can impact the physical world. Because algorithms are often considered to be neutral and unbiased, they can inaccurately project greater authority than human expertise (in part due to the psychological phenomenon of [automation bias](/wiki/Automation_bias "Automation bias")), and in some cases, reliance on algorithms can displace human responsibility for their outcomes, without [last mile](/wiki/Last_Mile_(artificial_intelligence) "Last Mile (artificial intelligence)") thinking. Bias can enter into algorithmic systems as a result of pre-existing cultural, social, or institutional expectations; by how features and labels are chosen; because of technical limitations of their design; or by being used in unanticipated contexts or by audiences who are not considered in the software's initial design.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
As algorithms expand their ability to organize society, politics, institutions, and behavior, sociologists have become concerned with the ways in which unanticipated output and manipulation of data can impact the physical world. Because algorithms are often considered to be neutral and unbiased, they can inaccurately project greater authority than human expertise (in part due to the psychological phenomenon of [automation bias](/wiki/Automation_bias "Automation bias")), and in some cases, reliance on algorithms can displace human responsibility for their outcomes, without [last mile](/wiki/Last_Mile_(artificial_intelligence) "Last Mile (artificial intelligence)") thinking. Bias can enter into algorithmic systems as a result of pre-existing cultural, social, or institutional expectations; by how features and labels are chosen; because of technical limitations of their design; or by being used in unanticipated contexts or by audiences who are not considered in the software's initial design.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Algorithmic bias has been cited in cases ranging from election outcomes to the spread of [online hate speech](/wiki/Online_hate_speech "Online hate speech"). It has also arisen in criminal justice,[[6]](#cite_note-6) healthcare, and hiring, compounding existing racial, socioeconomic, and gender biases. The relative inability of facial recognition technology to accurately identify darker-skinned faces has been linked to multiple wrongful arrests of black men, an issue stemming from imbalanced datasets. Problems in understanding, researching, and discovering algorithmic bias persist due to the proprietary nature of algorithms, which are typically treated as trade secrets. Even when full transparency is provided, the complexity of certain algorithms poses a barrier to understanding their functioning. Furthermore, algorithms may change, or respond to input or output in ways that cannot be anticipated or easily reproduced for analysis. In many cases, even within a single website or application, there is no single "algorithm" to examine, but a network of many interrelated programs and data inputs, even between users of the same service.

A 2021 survey identified multiple forms of algorithmic bias, including historical, representation, and measurement biases, each of which can contribute to unfair outcomes.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
## Definitions

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/A_computer_program_for_evaluating_forestry_opportunities_under_three_investment_criteria_%281969%29_%2820385500690%29.jpg/330px-A_computer_program_for_evaluating_forestry_opportunities_under_three_investment_criteria_%281969%29_%2820385500690%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:A_computer_program_for_evaluating_forestry_opportunities_under_three_investment_criteria_(1969)_(20385500690).jpg)

A 1969 diagram for how a simple computer program makes decisions, illustrating a very simple algorithm

Algorithms are [difficult to define](/wiki/Algorithm_characterizations "Algorithm characterizations"),[[8]](#cite_note-Striphas-8) but may be generally understood as lists of instructions that determine how programs read, collect, process, and analyze [data](/wiki/Data "Data") to generate a usable output.[[9]](#cite_note-Cormen-9): 13 For a rigorous technical introduction, see [Algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm"). Advances in [computer hardware](/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") and software have led to an increased capability to process, store and transmit data. This has in turn made the design and adoption of technologies such as [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") and [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") technically and commercially feasible.[[10]](#cite_note-Kitchin-10): 14–15 By analyzing and processing data, algorithms are the backbone of search engines,[[11]](#cite_note-GoogleAlgorithms-11) social media websites,[[12]](#cite_note-Luckerson-12) recommendation engines,[[13]](#cite_note-Vanderbilt-13) online retail,[[14]](#cite_note-AngwinMattu-14) online advertising,[[15]](#cite_note-Livingstone-15) and more.[[16]](#cite_note-Hickman-16)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
Algorithms are [difficult to define](/wiki/Algorithm_characterizations "Algorithm characterizations"),[[8]](#cite_note-Striphas-8) but may be generally understood as lists of instructions that determine how programs read, collect, process, and analyze [data](/wiki/Data "Data") to generate a usable output.[[9]](#cite_note-Cormen-9): 13 For a rigorous technical introduction, see [Algorithms](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm"). Advances in [computer hardware](/wiki/Computer_hardware "Computer hardware") and software have led to an increased capability to process, store and transmit data. This has in turn made the design and adoption of technologies such as [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") and [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") technically and commercially feasible.[[10]](#cite_note-Kitchin-10): 14–15 By analyzing and processing data, algorithms are the backbone of search engines,[[11]](#cite_note-GoogleAlgorithms-11) social media websites,[[12]](#cite_note-Luckerson-12) recommendation engines,[[13]](#cite_note-Vanderbilt-13) online retail,[[14]](#cite_note-AngwinMattu-14) online advertising,[[15]](#cite_note-Livingstone-15) and more.[[16]](#cite_note-Hickman-16)

Contemporary [social scientists](/wiki/Social_science "Social science") are concerned with algorithmic processes embedded into hardware and software applications because of their political and social impact, and question the underlying assumptions of an algorithm's neutrality.[[17]](#cite_note-Seaver-17): 2[[18]](#cite_note-Graham-18): 563[[19]](#cite_note-Tewell-19): 294[[20]](#cite_note-20) The term *algorithmic bias* describes systematic and repeatable errors that create unfair outcomes, such as privileging one arbitrary group of users over others. For example, a [credit score](/wiki/Credit_score "Credit score") algorithm may deny a loan without being unfair, if it is consistently weighing relevant financial criteria. If the algorithm recommends loans to one group of users, but denies loans to another set of nearly identical users based on unrelated criteria, and if this behavior can be repeated across multiple occurrences, an algorithm can be described as *biased*.[[21]](#cite_note-FriedmanNissenbaum-21): 332 This bias may be intentional or unintentional (for example, it can come from biased data obtained from a worker that previously did the job the algorithm is going to do from now on).

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
## Methods

Bias can be introduced to an algorithm in several ways. During the assemblage of a dataset, data may be collected, digitized, adapted, and entered into a [database](/wiki/Database "Database") according to human-designed [cataloging](/wiki/Cataloging "Cataloging") criteria.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 3 Next, programmers assign priorities, or [hierarchies](/wiki/Hierarchy "Hierarchy"), for how a program assesses and sorts that data. This requires human decisions about how data is categorized, and which data is included or discarded.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 4 Some algorithms collect their own data based on human-selected criteria, which can also reflect the bias of human designers.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 8 Other algorithms may reinforce stereotypes and preferences as they process and display "relevant" data for human users, for example, by selecting information based on previous choices of a similar user or group of users.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 6

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
Bias can be introduced to an algorithm in several ways. During the assemblage of a dataset, data may be collected, digitized, adapted, and entered into a [database](/wiki/Database "Database") according to human-designed [cataloging](/wiki/Cataloging "Cataloging") criteria.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 3 Next, programmers assign priorities, or [hierarchies](/wiki/Hierarchy "Hierarchy"), for how a program assesses and sorts that data. This requires human decisions about how data is categorized, and which data is included or discarded.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 4 Some algorithms collect their own data based on human-selected criteria, which can also reflect the bias of human designers.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 8 Other algorithms may reinforce stereotypes and preferences as they process and display "relevant" data for human users, for example, by selecting information based on previous choices of a similar user or group of users.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 6

Beyond assembling and processing data, bias can emerge as a result of design.[[23]](#cite_note-TowCenter-23) For example, algorithms that determine the allocation of resources or scrutiny (such as determining school placements) may inadvertently discriminate against a category when determining risk based on similar users (as in credit scores).[[24]](#cite_note-Lipartito-24): 36 Meanwhile, recommendation engines that work by associating users with similar users, or that make use of inferred marketing traits, might rely on inaccurate associations that reflect broad ethnic, gender, socio-economic, or racial stereotypes. Another example comes from determining criteria for what is included and excluded from results. These criteria could present unanticipated outcomes for search results, such as with flight-recommendation software that omits flights that do not follow the sponsoring airline's flight paths.[[23]](#cite_note-TowCenter-23) Algorithms may also display an *uncertainty bias*, offering more confident assessments when larger [data sets](/wiki/Data_set "Data set") are available. This can skew algorithmic processes toward results that more closely correspond with larger samples, which may disregard data from underrepresented populations.[[25]](#cite_note-GoodmanFlaxman2016-25): 4

text: ## History

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
### Early critiques

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Used_Punchcard_%285151286161%29.jpg/330px-Used_Punchcard_%285151286161%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Used_Punchcard_(5151286161).jpg)

This card was used to load software into an old mainframe computer. Each byte (the letter 'A', for example) is entered by punching holes. Though contemporary computers are more complex, they reflect this human decision-making process in collecting and processing data.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 70[[27]](#cite_note-Goffrey-27): 16

The earliest computer programs were designed to mimic human reasoning and deductions, and were deemed to be functioning when they successfully and consistently reproduced that human logic. In his 1976 book *[Computer Power and Human Reason](/wiki/Computer_Power_and_Human_Reason "Computer Power and Human Reason")*, [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") pioneer [Joseph Weizenbaum](/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum "Joseph Weizenbaum") suggested that bias could arise both from the data used in a program, but also from the way a program is coded.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 149

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
The earliest computer programs were designed to mimic human reasoning and deductions, and were deemed to be functioning when they successfully and consistently reproduced that human logic. In his 1976 book *[Computer Power and Human Reason](/wiki/Computer_Power_and_Human_Reason "Computer Power and Human Reason")*, [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") pioneer [Joseph Weizenbaum](/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum "Joseph Weizenbaum") suggested that bias could arise both from the data used in a program, but also from the way a program is coded.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 149

Weizenbaum wrote that [programs](/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program") are a sequence of rules created by humans for a computer to follow. By following those rules consistently, such programs "embody law",[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 40 that is, enforce a specific way to solve problems. The rules a computer follows are based on the assumptions of a computer programmer for how these problems might be solved. That means the code could incorporate the programmer's imagination of how the world works, including their biases and expectations.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 109 While a computer program can incorporate bias in this way, Weizenbaum also noted that any data fed to a machine additionally reflects "human decision making processes" as data is being selected.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 70, 105

Finally, he noted that machines might also transfer good information with [unintended consequences](/wiki/Unintended_consequence "Unintended consequence") if users are unclear about how to interpret the results.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 65 Weizenbaum warned against trusting decisions made by computer programs that a user doesn't understand, comparing such faith to a tourist who can find his way to a hotel room exclusively by turning left or right on a coin toss. Crucially, the tourist has no basis of understanding how or why he arrived at his destination, and a successful arrival does not mean the process is accurate or reliable.[[26]](#cite_note-Weizenbaum1976-26): 226

An early example of algorithmic bias resulted in as many as 60 women and ethnic minorities denied entry to [St. George's Hospital Medical School](/wiki/St_George%27s,_University_of_London "St George's, University of London") per year from 1982 to 1986, based on implementation of a new computer-guidance assessment system that denied entry to women and men with "foreign-sounding names" based on historical trends in admissions.[[28]](#cite_note-LowryMacpherson-28) While many schools at the time employed similar biases in their selection process, St. George was most notable for automating said bias through the use of an algorithm, thus gaining the attention of people on a much wider scale.

In recent years, as algorithms increasingly rely on machine learning methods applied to real-world data, algorithmic bias has become more prevalent due to inherent biases within the data itself. For instance, facial recognition systems have been shown to misidentify individuals from marginalized groups at significantly higher rates than white individuals, highlighting how biases in training datasets manifest in deployed systems.[[29]](#cite_note-29) A 2018 study by [Joy Buolamwini](/wiki/Joy_Buolamwini "Joy Buolamwini") and [Timnit Gebru](/wiki/Timnit_Gebru "Timnit Gebru") found that commercial facial recognition technologies exhibited error rates of up to 35% when identifying darker-skinned women, compared to less than 1% for lighter-skinned men.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

Algorithmic biases are not only technical failures but often reflect systemic inequities embedded in historical and societal data. Researchers and critics, such as [Cathy O'Neil](/wiki/Cathy_O%27Neil "Cathy O'Neil") in her book *[Weapons of Math Destruction](/wiki/Weapons_of_Math_Destruction "Weapons of Math Destruction")* (2016), emphasize that these biases can amplify existing social inequalities under the guise of objectivity. O'Neil argues that opaque, [automated decision-making](/wiki/Automated_decision-making "Automated decision-making") processes in areas such as credit scoring, predictive policing, and education can reinforce discriminatory practices while appearing neutral or scientific.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
### Contemporary critiques and responses

Though well-designed algorithms frequently determine outcomes that are equally (or more) equitable than the decisions of human beings, cases of bias still occur, and are difficult to predict and analyze.[[32]](#cite_note-Miller-32) The complexity of analyzing algorithmic bias has grown alongside the complexity of programs and their design. Decisions made by one designer, or team of designers, may be obscured among the many pieces of code created for a single program; over time these decisions and their collective impact on the program's output may be forgotten.[[33]](#cite_note-Introna1-33): 115 In theory, these biases may create new patterns of behavior, or "scripts", in relationship to specific technologies as the code [interacts](/wiki/Cybernetics "Cybernetics") with other elements of society.[[34]](#cite_note-Bogost-34) Biases may also impact how society shapes itself around the [data points](/wiki/Data_point "Data point") that algorithms require. For example, if data shows a high number of arrests in a particular area, an algorithm may assign more police patrols to that area, which could lead to more arrests.[[35]](#cite_note-IntronaWood-35): 180

The decisions of algorithmic programs can be seen as more authoritative than the decisions of the human beings they are meant to assist,[[36]](#cite_note-Introna2-36): 15 a process described by author [Clay Shirky](/wiki/Clay_Shirky "Clay Shirky") as "algorithmic authority".[[37]](#cite_note-ShirkyAuthority-37) Shirky uses the term to describe "the decision to regard as authoritative an unmanaged process of extracting value from diverse, untrustworthy sources", such as search results.[[37]](#cite_note-ShirkyAuthority-37) This neutrality can also be misrepresented by the language used by experts and the media when results are presented to the public. For example, a list of news items selected and presented as "trending" or "popular" may be created based on significantly wider criteria than just their popularity.[[22]](#cite_note-Gillespie_et_al-22): 14

Because of their convenience and authority, algorithms are theorized as a means of delegating responsibility away from humans.[[36]](#cite_note-Introna2-36): 16[[38]](#cite_note-Ziewitz1-38): 6 This can have the effect of reducing alternative options, compromises, or flexibility.[[36]](#cite_note-Introna2-36): 16 Sociologist [Scott Lash](/wiki/Scott_Lash "Scott Lash") has critiqued algorithms as a new form of "generative power", in that they are a virtual means of generating actual ends. Where previously human behavior generated data to be collected and studied, powerful algorithms increasingly could shape and define human behaviors.[[39]](#cite_note-Lash-39): 71

While blind adherence to algorithmic decisions is a concern, an opposite issue arises when human decision-makers exhibit "selective adherence" to algorithmic advice. In such cases, individuals accept recommendations that align with their preexisting beliefs and disregard those that do not, thereby perpetuating existing biases and undermining the fairness objectives of algorithmic interventions. Consequently, incorporating fair algorithmic tools into decision-making processes does not automatically eliminate human biases.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

Concerns over the impact of algorithms on society have led to the creation of working groups in organizations such as [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") and [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"), which have co-created a working group named Fairness, Accountability,
and Transparency in Machine Learning.[[41]](#cite_note-Garcia-41): 115 Ideas from Google have included community groups that patrol the outcomes of algorithms and vote to control or restrict outputs they deem to have negative consequences.[[41]](#cite_note-Garcia-41): 117 In recent years, the study of the Fairness, Accountability,
and Transparency (FAT) of algorithms has emerged as its own interdisciplinary research area with an annual conference called FAccT.[[42]](#cite_note-42) Critics have suggested that FAT initiatives cannot serve effectively as independent watchdogs when many are funded by corporations building the systems being studied.[[43]](#cite_note-Ochigame-43)

NIST's AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and its 2024 Generative AI Profile provide practical guidance for governing and measuring bias mitigation in AI systems.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

title: Algorithmic bias
text: ## Types

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
### Pre-existing

Pre-existing bias in an algorithm is a consequence of underlying social and institutional [ideologies](/wiki/Ideology "Ideology"). Bias can be placed intentionally or accidentally.[[21]](#cite_note-FriedmanNissenbaum-21): 334[[19]](#cite_note-Tewell-19): 294Poorly selected input data, or simply data from a biased source, will influence the outcomes created by machines.[[27]](#cite_note-Goffrey-27): 17 Encoding pre-existing bias into software can preserve social and institutional bias, and, without correction, could be replicated in all future uses of that algorithm.[[33]](#cite_note-Introna1-33): 116[[38]](#cite_note-Ziewitz1-38): 8

An example of this form of bias is the British Nationality Act Program, designed to automate the evaluation of new British citizens after the 1981 [British Nationality Act](/wiki/British_Nationality_Act "British Nationality Act").[[21]](#cite_note-FriedmanNissenbaum-21): 341 The program accurately reflected the tenets of the law, which stated that "a man is the father of only his legitimate children, whereas a woman is the mother of all her children, legitimate or not."[[21]](#cite_note-FriedmanNissenbaum-21): 341[[45]](#cite_note-SergotEtAl-45): 375 In its attempt to transfer a particular logic into an algorithmic process, the BNAP inscribed the logic of the British Nationality Act into its algorithm, which would perpetuate it even if the act was eventually repealed.[[21]](#cite_note-FriedmanNissenbaum-21): 342

Another source of bias, which has been called "label choice bias",[[46]](#cite_note-brookings.edu-46) arises when proxy measures are used to train algorithms, that build in bias against certain groups. For example, a widely used algorithm predicted health care costs as a proxy for health care needs, and used predictions to allocate resources to help patients with complex health needs. This introduced bias because Black patients have lower costs, even when they are just as unhealthy as White patients[[47]](#cite_note-47) Solutions to the "label choice bias" aim to match the actual target (what the algorithm is predicting) more closely to the ideal target (what researchers want the algorithm to predict), so for the prior example, instead of predicting cost, researchers would focus on the variable of healthcare needs which is rather more significant. Adjusting the target led to almost double the number of Black patients being selected for the program.[[46]](#cite_note-brookings.edu-46)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
### Machine learning bias

Machine learning bias refers to systematic and unfair disparities in the output of machine learning algorithms. These biases can manifest in various ways and are often a reflection of the data used to train these algorithms. Some common types of machine learning bias include:

- Data bias: Training data may under‑represent certain groups (e.g., minority populations), contain historical inequalities, or be collected in skewed ways, leading the model to perform worse or behave unfairly for those groups.[[48]](#cite_note-48)
- Label bias: Human‑provided labels can encode subjective judgments or prejudices (for example, what is labeled as "risky," "toxic," or "qualified"), so the model learns and amplifies those judgments.
- Measurement bias: Proxies or measurements used for important concepts (like "creditworthiness" or "[job performance](/wiki/Job_performance "Job performance")") may be noisy or systematically distorted for some groups, which then distorts predictions.
- Algorithmic bias: Even with relatively balanced data, modeling choices (loss functions, thresholds, optimization objectives) can prioritize overall accuracy over fairness, leaving some subgroups with consistently worse outcomes.[[49]](#cite_note-:6-49)
- Deployment bias: A model used outside the context it was designed for (e.g., a model trained on adults applied to children, or one trained in one country deployed in another) can generate biased results because the environment and population differ.
