The United States has no general legislation controlling algorithmic bias, approaching the problem through various state and federal laws that might vary by industry, sector, and by how an algorithm is used.[[220]](#cite_note-Singer-220) Many policies are self-enforced or controlled by the [Federal Trade Commission](/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission").[[220]](#cite_note-Singer-220) In 2016, the Obama administration released the [National Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Strategic Plan](/w/index.php?title=National_Artificial_Intelligence_Research_and_Development_Strategic_Plan&action=edit&redlink=1 "National Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Strategic Plan (page does not exist)"),[[221]](#cite_note-ObamaAdmin-221) which was intended to guide policymakers toward a critical assessment of algorithms. It recommended researchers to "design these systems so that their actions and decision-making are transparent and easily interpretable by humans, and thus can be examined for any bias they may contain, rather than just learning and repeating these biases". Intended only as guidance, the report did not create any legal precedent.[[222]](#cite_note-NSTC-222): 26

In 2017, [New York City](/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") passed the first [algorithmic accountability](/wiki/Algorithmic_accountability "Algorithmic accountability") bill in the United States.[[223]](#cite_note-Kirchner-223) The bill, which went into effect on January 1, 2018, required "the creation of a task force that provides recommendations on how information on agency automated decision systems may be shared with the public, and how agencies may address instances where people are harmed by agency automated decision systems."[[224]](#cite_note-NYC-224) In 2023, New York City implemented a law requiring employers using automated hiring tools to conduct independent "bias audits" and publish the results. This law marked one of the first legally mandated transparency measures for AI systems used in employment decisions in the United States.[[225]](#cite_note-225) The task force is required to present findings and recommendations for further regulatory action in 2019.[[226]](#cite_note-Powles-226)
On February 11, 2019, according to [Executive Order 13859](/w/index.php?title=Executive_Order_13859&action=edit&redlink=1 "Executive Order 13859 (page does not exist)"), the federal government unveiled the "American AI Initiative", a comprehensive strategy to maintain U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. The initiative highlights the importance of sustained AI research and development, ethical standards, workforce training, and the protection of critical AI technologies.[[227]](#cite_note-227) This aligns with broader efforts to ensure transparency, accountability, and innovation in AI systems across public and private sectors.

This law marked one of the first legally mandated transparency measures for AI systems used in employment decisions in the United States.[[225]](#cite_note-225) The task force is required to present findings and recommendations for further regulatory action in 2019.[[226]](#cite_note-Powles-226)
On February 11, 2019, according to [Executive Order 13859](/w/index.php?title=Executive_Order_13859&action=edit&redlink=1 "Executive Order 13859 (page does not exist)"), the federal government unveiled the "American AI Initiative", a comprehensive strategy to maintain U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence. The initiative highlights the importance of sustained AI research and development, ethical standards, workforce training, and the protection of critical AI technologies.[[227]](#cite_note-227) This aligns with broader efforts to ensure transparency, accountability, and innovation in AI systems across public and private sectors.

Furthermore, on October 30, 2023, the president signed [Executive Order 14110](/wiki/Executive_Order_14110 "Executive Order 14110"), which emphasizes the safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of artificial intelligence (AI). The order outlines a coordinated, government-wide approach to harness AI's potential while mitigating its risks, including fraud, discrimination, and national security threats. An important point in the commitment is promoting responsible innovation and collaboration across sectors to ensure that AI benefits society as a whole.[[228]](#cite_note-228) With this order, President Joe Biden mandated the federal government to create best practices for companies to optimize AI's benefits and minimize its harms.[[229]](#cite_note-229)

title: Algorithmic bias
text:
### India

On July 31, 2018, a draft of the Personal Data Bill was presented.[[230]](#cite_note-230) The draft proposes standards for the storage, processing and transmission of data. While it does not use the term algorithm, it makes for provisions for "harm resulting from any processing or any kind of processing undertaken by the fiduciary". It defines "any denial or withdrawal of a service, benefit or good resulting from an evaluative decision about the data principal" or "any discriminatory treatment" as a source of harm that could arise from improper use of data. It also makes special provisions for people of "Intersex status".[[231]](#cite_note-231)

title: AIOps
text:
Artificial intelligence in IT operations

**AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations)** refers to the use of [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"), and [big data analytics](/wiki/Big_data "Big data") to automate and enhance [data center management](/wiki/Data_center_management "Data center management"). It helps organizations manage complex IT environments by detecting, diagnosing, and resolving issues more efficiently than traditional methods.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: AIOps
text:
## History

AIOps was first defined by [Gartner](/wiki/Gartner "Gartner") in 2016,[[3]](#cite_note-3) combining "artificial intelligence" and "IT operations" to describe the application of AI and machine learning to enhance IT operations. This concept was introduced to address the increasing complexity and data volume in IT environments, aiming to automate processes such as [event correlation](/wiki/Event_correlation "Event correlation"), [anomaly detection](/wiki/Anomaly_detection "Anomaly detection"), and causality determination.

title: AIOps
text:
## Definition

AIOps refers to multi-layered, complex technology platforms that enhance and automate IT operations by using machine learning and analytics to analyze the large amounts of data collected from various [DevOps](/wiki/DevOps "DevOps") devices and tools, automatically identifying and responding to issues in real-time.[[4]](#cite_note-4) AIOps represents a shift from isolated IT data to aggregated observational data (e.g., job logs and monitoring systems) and interaction data (such as ticketing, events, or incident records) within a big data platform.[[5]](#cite_note-5) AIOps applies machine learning and analytics to this data, resulting in continuous visibility that, when combined with automation, can lead to ongoing improvements.[[6]](#cite_note-6) AIOps connects three IT disciplines ([automation](/wiki/Automation "Automation"), [service management](/wiki/Service_management "Service management"), and performance management) to achieve continuous visibility and improvement. This new approach in modern, accelerated, and hyper-scaled IT environments leverages advances in machine learning and big data to overcome previous limitations.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

title: AIOps
text:
## Components

AIOps includes, but is not limited to, the following processes and techniques:

- [Anomaly Detection](/wiki/Anomaly_detection "Anomaly detection")[[8]](#cite_note-8)
- [Log Analysis](/wiki/Log_analysis "Log analysis")[[9]](#cite_note-9)
- [Root Cause Analysis](/wiki/Root_cause_analysis "Root cause analysis")[[10]](#cite_note-10)
- [Cohort Analysis](/wiki/Cohort_analysis "Cohort analysis")[[11]](#cite_note-11)
- [Event Correlation](/wiki/Event_correlation "Event correlation")[[12]](#cite_note-12)
- [Predictive Analytics](/wiki/Predictive_analytics "Predictive analytics")[[13]](#cite_note-13)
- Hardware Failure Prediction[[14]](#cite_note-14)
- Automated Remediation[[15]](#cite_note-15)
- [Performance Prediction](/wiki/Performance_prediction "Performance prediction")[[16]](#cite_note-16)
- [Incident Management](/wiki/Incident_management "Incident management")[[17]](#cite_note-:0-17)
- Causality Determination[[18]](#cite_note-18)
- Queue Management[[19]](#cite_note-19)
- Resource Scheduling and Optimization[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Predictive Capacity Management[[17]](#cite_note-:0-17)
- [Resource Allocation](/wiki/Resource_allocation_(computer) "Resource allocation (computer)")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- [Service Quality](/wiki/Service_quality "Service quality") Monitoring[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- [Deployment](/wiki/Deployment_management "Deployment management") and [Integration Testing](/wiki/Integration_testing "Integration testing")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- [System Configuration](/wiki/System_configuration "System configuration")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Auto-diagnosis and Problem Localization[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Efficient ML Training and [Inferencing](/wiki/Inference "Inference")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Using LLMs for [Cloud](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") Ops[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Auto Service Healing[[17]](#cite_note-:0-17)
- [Data Center Management](/wiki/Data_center_management "Data center management")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- [Customer Support](/wiki/Customer_support "Customer support")[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)
- Security and Privacy in Cloud Operations[[20]](#cite_note-:1-20)

title: AIOps
text:
## Comparison with DevOps

AIOps is increasingly compared with DevOps in terms of impact on operational efficiency. While DevOps focuses on collaboration between development and operations teams to accelerate software delivery, AIOps integrates artificial intelligence to enhance monitoring, automation, and predictive capabilities. Various industry analyses have explored the similarities and differences between the two approaches, including discussions on how organizations can combine them to improve incident management and resource optimization.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

title: AIOps
text:
## Results

AI optimizes [IT](/wiki/IT "IT") operations in five ways: First, intelligent monitoring powered by AI helps identify potential issues before they cause outages, improving metrics like Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) by 15-20%. Second, performance data analysis and insights enable quick decision-making by ingesting and analyzing large data sets in real time. Third, AI-driven automated infrastructure optimization efficiently allocates resources and thereby reducing cloud costs. Fourth, enhanced IT service management reduces critical incidents by over 50% through AI-driven end-to-end service management. Lastly, intelligent task automation accelerates problem resolution and automates remedial actions with minimal human intervention.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

title: AIOps
text:
## AIOps vs. MLOps

AIOps tools use big data analytics, machine learning algorithms, and [predictive analytics](/wiki/Predictive_analytics "Predictive analytics") to detect anomalies, correlate events, and provide proactive insights. This automation reduces the burden on IT teams, allowing them to focus on strategic tasks rather than routine operational issues. AIOps is widely used by IT operations teams, [DevOps](/wiki/DevOps "DevOps"), network administrators, and [IT service management](/wiki/IT_service_management "IT service management") (ITSM) teams to enhance visibility and enable quicker incident resolution in hybrid cloud environments, data centers, and other IT infrastructures.[[23]](#cite_note-auto-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

In contrast to [MLOps](/wiki/MLOps "MLOps") (Machine Learning Operations), which focuses on the lifecycle management and operational aspects of machine learning models, AIOps focuses on optimizing IT operations using a variety of analytics and AI-driven techniques. While both disciplines rely on AI and data-driven methods, AIOps primarily targets IT operations, whereas MLOps is concerned with the deployment, monitoring, and maintenance of ML models.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)

title: 80 Million Tiny Images
text:
Dataset for training machine-learning systems

**80 Million Tiny Images** is a [dataset](/wiki/Dataset "Dataset") intended for training [machine-learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") systems constructed by Antonio Torralba, [Rob Fergus](/wiki/Rob_Fergus "Rob Fergus"), and [William T. Freeman](/wiki/William_T._Freeman "William T. Freeman") in a collaboration between [MIT](/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") and [New York University](/wiki/New_York_University "New York University"). It was published in 2008.

The dataset has size 760 [GB](/wiki/Gigabyte "Gigabyte"). It contains 79,302,017 32×32-pixel color images, scaled down from images scraped from the [World Wide Web](/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web") over 8 months. The images are classified into 75,062 classes. Each class is a non-abstract noun in [WordNet](/wiki/WordNet "WordNet"). Images may appear in more than one class. The dataset was motivated by non-parametric models of neural activations in the [visual cortex](/wiki/Visual_cortex "Visual cortex") upon seeing images.[[1]](#cite_note-Torralba2008-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The [CIFAR-10](/wiki/CIFAR-10 "CIFAR-10") dataset uses a subset of the images in this dataset, but with independently generated labels, as the original labels were not reliable. The CIFAR-10 set has 6000 examples of each of 10 classes, and the CIFAR-100 set has 600 examples of each of 100 non-overlapping classes.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

title: 80 Million Tiny Images
text:
## Construction

It was first reported in a [technical report](/wiki/Technical_report "Technical report") in April 2007, during the middle of the construction process, when there were only 73 million images.[[4]](#cite_note-4) The full dataset was published in 2008.[[1]](#cite_note-Torralba2008-1)

They began with all 75,846 non-abstract nouns in [WordNet](/wiki/WordNet "WordNet"), and then for each of these nouns, they scraped 7 image search engines: [Altavista](/wiki/Altavista "Altavista"), [Ask.com](/wiki/Ask.com "Ask.com"), [Flickr](/wiki/Flickr "Flickr"), [Cydral](/w/index.php?title=Cydral&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cydral (page does not exist)"), [Google](/wiki/Google "Google"), [Picsearch](/wiki/Picsearch "Picsearch"), and [Webshots](/wiki/Webshots "Webshots"). After 8 months of scraping, they obtained 97,245,098 images. Since they did not have enough storage, they downsized the images to 32×32 as they were scraped. After gathering, they removed images with zero variance and intra-word duplicate images, resulting in the final dataset.

Out of the 75,846 nouns, only 75,062 classes had *any* results, so the other nouns did not appear in the final dataset.

The number of images per noun follows a [Zipf-like distribution](/wiki/Zipf%27s_law "Zipf's law"), with 1056 images per noun on average. To prevent a few nouns taking up too many images, they put an upper bound of at most 3000 images per noun.[[1]](#cite_note-Torralba2008-1)

title: 80 Million Tiny Images
text:
## Retirement

The 80 Million Tiny Images dataset was retired from use by its creators in 2020,[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5) after a paper by researchers [Abeba Birhane](/wiki/Abeba_Birhane "Abeba Birhane") and Vinay Prabhu found that some of the labeling of several publicly available image datasets, including 80 Million Tiny Images, contained racist and misogynistic slurs which were causing models trained on them to exhibit racial and sexual bias. The dataset also contained offensive images.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) Following the release of the paper, the dataset's creators removed the dataset from distribution, and requested that other researchers not use it for further research and to delete their copies of the dataset.[[5]](#cite_note-:0-5)

**XLA** (**Accelerated Linear Algebra**) is an [open-source](/wiki/Open-source "Open-source") [compiler](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") for [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") developed by the OpenXLA project.[[1]](#cite_note-1) XLA is designed to improve the performance of machine learning models by optimizing the computation graphs at a lower level, making it particularly useful for large-scale computations and high-performance machine learning models. Key features of XLA include:[[2]](#cite_note-2)

- Compilation of Computation Graphs: Compiles computation graphs into efficient [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code").
- Optimization Techniques: Applies operation fusion, memory optimization, and other techniques.
- Hardware Support: Optimizes models for various hardware, including [CPUs](/wiki/CPU "CPU"), [GPUs](/wiki/GPU "GPU"), and [NPUs](/wiki/Neural_processing_unit "Neural processing unit").
- Improved Model Execution Time: Aims to reduce machine learning models' execution time for both training and inference.
- Seamless Integration: Can be used with existing machine learning code with minimal changes.

XLA represents a significant step in optimizing machine learning models, providing developers with tools to enhance computational efficiency and performance.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

title: Accelerated Linear Algebra
text:
## OpenXLA Project

**OpenXLA Project** is an open-source machine learning compiler and infrastructure initiative intended to provide a common set of tools for compiling and deploying machine learning models across different frameworks and hardware platforms. It provides a modular compilation stack that can be used by major deep learning frameworks like [JAX](/wiki/JAX_(software) "JAX (software)"), [PyTorch](/wiki/PyTorch "PyTorch"), and [TensorFlow](/wiki/TensorFlow "TensorFlow"). The project focuses on supplying shared components for optimization, portability, and execution across CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators. Its design emphasizes interoperability between frameworks and a standardized set of representations for model computation.

title: Accelerated Linear Algebra
text:
## Components

The OpenXLA ecosystem includes several core components:

- **XLA** – A deep learning compiler that optimizes computational graphs for multiple hardware targets.
- **PJRT** – A runtime interface that allows different back-ends to connect to XLA through a consistent [API](/wiki/API "API").
- **StableHLO** – A high-level operator set intended to serve as a stable, portable representation for ML models across compilers and frameworks.
- **Shardy** – An MLIR-based system for describing and transforming models that run in distributed or multi-device environments.
- Additional profiling, testing, and integration tools maintained under the OpenXLA organization.

title: Accelerated Linear Algebra
text:
## Users and adopters

Several machine learning frameworks can use or interoperate with OpenXLA components, including JAX, TensorFlow, and parts of the PyTorch ecosystem. The project is developed with participation from multiple hardware and software organizations that contribute back-end integrations, testing, or specifications for their devices. This includes [Alibaba](/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group"), [Amazon Web Services](/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services "Amazon Web Services"), [AMD](/wiki/AMD "AMD"), Anyscale, [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), Arm, [Cerebras](/wiki/Cerebras "Cerebras"), [Google](/wiki/Google "Google"), [Graphcore](/wiki/Graphcore "Graphcore"), [Hugging Face](/wiki/Hugging_Face "Hugging Face"), [Intel](/wiki/Intel "Intel"), [Meta](/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms"), [NVIDIA](/wiki/Nvidia "Nvidia") and [SiFive](/wiki/SiFive "SiFive").[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Governance

OpenXLA is developed as a community project with its work carried out in public repositories, discussion forums, and design meetings. Some components, such as StableHLO, began with stewardship from specific organizations and have outlined plans for more formal and distributed governance models as the project matures.

title: Accelerated Linear Algebra
text:
## History

The project was announced in 2022 as an effort to coordinate development of ML compiler technologies across major AI companies, notably: Alibaba, Amazon Web Services, AMD, Anyscale, Apple, Arm, Cerebras, Google, Graphcore, Hugging Face, Intel, Meta, NVIDIA and SiFive.. It consolidated the XLA compiler, introduced StableHLO as a portable operator set, and created a unified structure for additional tools. Development continues within multiple repositories under the OpenXLA umbrella. It was founded by Eugene Burmako, James Rubin, Magnus Hyttsten, Mehdi Amini, Navid Khajouei, and Thea Lamkin from Google's Machine Learning organization.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
1943 paper proposing artificial neural networks

"**A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity**" is a 1943 paper written by [Warren Sturgis McCulloch](/wiki/Warren_Sturgis_McCulloch "Warren Sturgis McCulloch") and [Walter Pitts](/wiki/Walter_Pitts "Walter Pitts"), published in the journal *[The Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics](/wiki/The_Bulletin_of_Mathematical_Biophysics "The Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics")*.[[1]](#cite_note-1) The paper proposed a mathematical model of the nervous system as a network of simple logical elements, later known as [artificial neurons](/wiki/Artificial_neuron "Artificial neuron"), or [McCulloch–Pitts neurons](/wiki/McCulloch%E2%80%93Pitts_neuron "McCulloch–Pitts neuron"). These neurons receive inputs, perform a weighted sum, and fire an output signal based on a threshold function. By connecting these units in various configurations, McCulloch and Pitts demonstrated that their model could perform all logical functions.

It is a seminal work in [cognitive science](/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science"), [computational neuroscience](/wiki/Computational_neuroscience "Computational neuroscience"), [computer science](/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), and [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"). It was a foundational result in [automata theory](/wiki/Automata_theory "Automata theory"). [John von Neumann](/wiki/John_von_Neumann "John von Neumann") cited it as a significant result.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

text:
### Previous work

The paper built upon several previous strands of work.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In the symbolic logic side, it built on the previous work by Carnap, Whitehead, and Russell. This was contributed by Walter Pitts, who had a strong proficiency with symbolic logic. Pitts provided mathematical and logical rigor to McCulloch’s vague ideas on psychons (atoms of psychological events) and circular causality.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

In the neuroscience side, it built on previous work by the mathematical biology research group centered around [Nicolas Rashevsky](/wiki/Nicolas_Rashevsky "Nicolas Rashevsky"), of which McCulloch was a member. The paper was published in the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, which was founded by Rashevsky in 1939. During the late 1930s, Rashevsky's research group was producing papers that had difficulty publishing in other journals at the time, so Rashevsky decided to found a new journal exclusively devoted to mathematical biophysics.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
In the neuroscience side, it built on previous work by the mathematical biology research group centered around [Nicolas Rashevsky](/wiki/Nicolas_Rashevsky "Nicolas Rashevsky"), of which McCulloch was a member. The paper was published in the *Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics*, which was founded by Rashevsky in 1939. During the late 1930s, Rashevsky's research group was producing papers that had difficulty publishing in other journals at the time, so Rashevsky decided to found a new journal exclusively devoted to mathematical biophysics.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Also in the Rashevsky's group was [Alston Scott Householder](/wiki/Alston_Scott_Householder "Alston Scott Householder"), who in 1941 published an abstract model of the steady-state activity of biological neural networks. The model, in modern language, is an artificial neural network with [ReLU](/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks) "Rectifier (neural networks)") activation function.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In a series of papers, Householder calculated the stable states of very simple networks: a chain, a circle, and a [bouquet](/wiki/Rose_(topology) "Rose (topology)"). Walter Pitts' first two papers formulated a mathematical theory of learning and conditioning. The next three were mathematical developments of Householder’s model.[[10]](#cite_note-:1-10)

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
Also in the Rashevsky's group was [Alston Scott Householder](/wiki/Alston_Scott_Householder "Alston Scott Householder"), who in 1941 published an abstract model of the steady-state activity of biological neural networks. The model, in modern language, is an artificial neural network with [ReLU](/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks) "Rectifier (neural networks)") activation function.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In a series of papers, Householder calculated the stable states of very simple networks: a chain, a circle, and a [bouquet](/wiki/Rose_(topology) "Rose (topology)"). Walter Pitts' first two papers formulated a mathematical theory of learning and conditioning. The next three were mathematical developments of Householder’s model.[[10]](#cite_note-:1-10)

In 1938, at age 15, Pitts ran away from home in Detroit and arrived in the [University of Chicago](/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"). Later, he walked into Rudolf Carnap's office with Carnap's book filled with corrections and suggested improvements. He started studying under Carnap and attending classes during 1938–1943. He wrote several early papers on neuronal network modelling and regularly attended Rashevsky's seminars in theoretical biology. The seminar attendants included Gerhard von Bonin and Householder. In 1940, von Bonin introduced Lettvin to McCulloch. In 1942, both Lettvin and Pitts had moved in with McCulloch's home.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
In 1938, at age 15, Pitts ran away from home in Detroit and arrived in the [University of Chicago](/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"). Later, he walked into Rudolf Carnap's office with Carnap's book filled with corrections and suggested improvements. He started studying under Carnap and attending classes during 1938–1943. He wrote several early papers on neuronal network modelling and regularly attended Rashevsky's seminars in theoretical biology. The seminar attendants included Gerhard von Bonin and Householder. In 1940, von Bonin introduced Lettvin to McCulloch. In 1942, both Lettvin and Pitts had moved in with McCulloch's home.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

McCulloch had been interested in circular causality from studies with [causalgia](/wiki/Complex_regional_pain_syndrome "Complex regional pain syndrome") after amputation, [epileptic](/wiki/Epilepsy "Epilepsy") activity of surgically isolated brain, and [Lorente de Nò](/wiki/Rafael_Lorente_de_N%C3%B3 "Rafael Lorente de Nó")'s research showing [recurrent neural networks](/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network "Recurrent neural network") are needed to explain [vestibular nystagmus](/wiki/Vestibulo-ocular_reflex "Vestibulo-ocular reflex"). He had difficulty with treating circular causality until Pitts demonstrated how it can be treated by the appropriate mathematical tools of [modular arithmetics](/wiki/Modular_arithmetic "Modular arithmetic") and symbolic logic.[[4]](#cite_note-number3-4)[[10]](#cite_note-:1-10)

Both authors' affiliation in the article was given as "University of Illinois, College of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry at the Illinois Neuropsychiatric Institute, University of Chicago, Chicago, U.S.A."

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
### Subsequent work

It was a foundational result in [automata theory](/wiki/Automata_theory "Automata theory"). [John von Neumann](/wiki/John_von_Neumann "John von Neumann") cited it as a significant result.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) This work led to work on neural networks and their link to [finite automata](/wiki/Finite_automata "Finite automata").[[12]](#cite_note-12) Kleene introduced the term *"regular"* for "regular language" in a 1951 technical report, where Kleene proved that [regular languages](/wiki/Regular_language "Regular language") are all that could be generated by neural networks, among other results. The term "regular" was meant to be suggestive of "regularly occurring events" that the neural net automaton must process and respond to.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

[Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") was influenced by McCulloch, built an early example of neural network [SNARC](/wiki/Stochastic_Neural_Analog_Reinforcement_Calculator "Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator") (1951), and did a PhD thesis on neural networks (1954).[[14]](#cite_note-14)

McCulloch was the chair to the ten [Macy conferences](/wiki/Macy_conferences "Macy conferences") (1946–1953) on "Circular Causal and Feedback Mechanisms in Biological and Social Systems". This was a key event in the beginning of [cybernetics](/wiki/Cybernetics "Cybernetics"), and what later became known as [cognitive science](/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science"). Pitts also attended the conferences.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity
text:
McCulloch was the chair to the ten [Macy conferences](/wiki/Macy_conferences "Macy conferences") (1946–1953) on "Circular Causal and Feedback Mechanisms in Biological and Social Systems". This was a key event in the beginning of [cybernetics](/wiki/Cybernetics "Cybernetics"), and what later became known as [cognitive science](/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science"). Pitts also attended the conferences.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In the 1943 paper, they described how memories can be formed by a neural network with loops in it, or alterable synapses, which are operating over time, and implements [logical universals](/wiki/Universal_quantification "Universal quantification") -- "there exists" and "for all". This was generalized for spatial objects, such as geometric figures, in their 1947 paper *How we know universals*.[[16]](#cite_note-16) Norbert Wiener found this a significant evidence for a general method for how animals recognizing objects, by scanning a scene from multiple transformations and finding a canonical representation. He hypothesized that this "scanning" activity is clocked by the [alpha wave](/wiki/Alpha_wave "Alpha wave"), which he mistakenly thought was tightly regulated at 10 Hz (instead of the 8 -- 13 Hz as modern research shows).[[17]](#cite_note-17)

title: AI data center
text:
Specialized data centers designed for artificial intelligence

An **AI data center** is a specialized [data center](/wiki/Data_center "Data center") facility designed for the computationally intensive tasks of training and running [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") (AI) and [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") models. Unlike general-purpose data centers, they are often optimized for the parallel processing demands of AI workloads, typically using hardware such as [AI accelerators](/wiki/AI_accelerator "AI accelerator") ([GPUs](/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit"), [TPUs](/wiki/Tensor_Processing_Unit "Tensor Processing Unit")) and high-speed [interconnects](/wiki/Interconnect_(integrated_circuits) "Interconnect (integrated circuits)").

The global push to construct these specialized facilities accelerated dramatically during the [AI boom](/wiki/AI_boom "AI boom") of the 2020s. In 2026, major tech companies were estimated to spend $650 billion on AI data centers.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Their purchases of [memory chips](/wiki/Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory"), particularly [High Bandwidth Memory](/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory"), led to a [global memory supply shortage](/wiki/2024%E2%80%932026_global_memory_supply_shortage "2024–2026 global memory supply shortage") amid a broader competition for semiconductors, power, and infrastructure.[[3]](#cite_note-reuters-ai-frenzy-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) About 70% of global [computer memory](/wiki/Computer_memory "Computer memory") production in [fiscal year](/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") 2026 has been purchased for AI data centers.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

In 2026, major tech companies were estimated to spend $650 billion on AI data centers.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Their purchases of [memory chips](/wiki/Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory"), particularly [High Bandwidth Memory](/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory"), led to a [global memory supply shortage](/wiki/2024%E2%80%932026_global_memory_supply_shortage "2024–2026 global memory supply shortage") amid a broader competition for semiconductors, power, and infrastructure.[[3]](#cite_note-reuters-ai-frenzy-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) About 70% of global [computer memory](/wiki/Computer_memory "Computer memory") production in [fiscal year](/wiki/Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") 2026 has been purchased for AI data centers.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

AI-focused data centers use around 60 kilowatts of electricity per [server rack](/wiki/Server_rack "Server rack"), while general-purpose data centers typically use around 10 kilowatts of electricity per rack.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-Leppert-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

By 2026, many U.S. communities had organized against the local construction of AI data centers, which can consume large amounts of power and water and generate heat, noise, and other pollutants. By July 2026, local community resistance had blocked the construction of AI data centers worth some $130 billion.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

title: AI data center
text:
## Operators

As of August 2025, [The Information](/wiki/The_Information_(website) "The Information (website)") tracked 18 planned or existing AI data centers in the United States, operated by [Amazon Web Services](/wiki/Amazon_Web_Services "Amazon Web Services"), [CoreWeave](/wiki/CoreWeave "CoreWeave"), Crusoe, [Meta](/wiki/Meta_Platforms "Meta Platforms"), [Microsoft](/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft")/[OpenAI](/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI"), [Oracle](/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation"), [Tesla](/wiki/Tesla,_Inc. "Tesla, Inc."), and [xAI](/wiki/XAI_(company) "XAI (company)").[[12]](#cite_note-12) Other AI data center operators include [Digital Realty](/wiki/Digital_Realty "Digital Realty") and [Alibaba](/wiki/Alibaba_Group "Alibaba Group").[[13]](#cite_note-Booth-13) Data centers are also being built in China, India, Europe,[[13]](#cite_note-Booth-13) Saudi Arabia,[[14]](#cite_note-14) and Canada.[[15]](#cite_note-15) *[The New Yorker](/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* described CoreWeave as the most prominent AI data center operator in the United States.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Two types of data center providers for machine learning have been noted in [news media](/wiki/News_media "News media"): hyperscalers and neoclouds. *[The Verge](/wiki/The_Verge "The Verge")* listed large technology companies such as Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon as hyperscalers.[[17]](#cite_note-Lopatto-17) *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* described neoclouds as "a new generation of data center providers". CoreWeave, Nebius, [Nscale](/wiki/NScale "NScale"), and Lambda have been described as examples of neoclouds.[[18]](#cite_note-Weise-18)

title: AI data center
text:
In January 2025, OpenAI, in partnership with Oracle and [Softbank](/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group"), announced the [Stargate](/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC") project, which as of September 2025 is composed of six built or proposed AI data centers in the United States.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In response to the Stargate project, [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") launched in October 2025 an AI data center on 1,200 acres of farmland in Indiana. This data center, known as Project Rainier, is one of the largest AI data centers in the world, with Amazon spending $11 billion on the project. Rainier is specifically intended for training and running machine learning models from [Anthropic](/wiki/Anthropic "Anthropic").[[20]](#cite_note-20) As of that time, this facility contains seven data centers (out of an estimated 30 planned) and will use 2.2 gigawatts of electricity (equivalent to 1 million households) and millions of gallons of water per year. Computer chips from [Annapurna Labs](/wiki/Annapurna_Labs "Annapurna Labs") and Anthropic, Trainium 2, were designed for use in such facilities. Amazon pumped millions of gallons of water out of the ground to construct the data center, and as of June 2025, Indiana state officials are investigating whether this [dewatering](/wiki/Dewatering "Dewatering") process led to dry wells for local residents.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In November 2025, Anthropic announced a partnership with Fluidstack to develop [artificial intelligence infrastructure](/wiki/AI_infrastructure "AI infrastructure") in the United States, including data centers in New York and Texas, worth $50 billion.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

title: AI data center
text:
In November 2025, Anthropic announced a partnership with Fluidstack to develop [artificial intelligence infrastructure](/wiki/AI_infrastructure "AI infrastructure") in the United States, including data centers in New York and Texas, worth $50 billion.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Other AI data center projects include the [Colossus supercomputer](/wiki/Colossus_(supercomputer) "Colossus (supercomputer)") from xAI, a Louisiana-based project from Meta, Hyperion, expected to use 5 GW of power, and a second Ohio-based Meta project, Prometheus, with a capacity of 1 GW.[[23]](#cite_note-23) A 3,200-acre AI data center, capable of 4.4-4.5 GW of power and located on the decommissioned [Homer City Generating Station](/wiki/Homer_City_Generating_Station "Homer City Generating Station"), is under construction as of 2025, and will use seven 30-acre gas generating stations supplied by [EQT](/wiki/EQT_Corporation "EQT Corporation").[[24]](#cite_note-Halper-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

As of December 2025, [CRH](/wiki/CRH_plc "CRH plc") is working on over 100 data centers in the United States.[[26]](#cite_note-Berg-26)

In 2025, [ExxonMobil](/wiki/ExxonMobil "ExxonMobil") and [NextEra](/wiki/NextEra_Energy "NextEra Energy") announced plans to build a data center powered by [natural gas](/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") and using [carbon capture technology](/wiki/Carbon_capture_and_storage "Carbon capture and storage"), with 1.2 GW of power capacity. They previously purchased 2,500 acres of land in the [Southeastern United States](/wiki/Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") and plan to market the data center to an artificial intelligence company.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

"Snowflake Inc.") and Cipher Mining.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

Several companies involved in [cryptocurrency mining](/wiki/Cryptocurrency_mining "Cryptocurrency mining"), such as [Bitdeer](/wiki/Bitdeer "Bitdeer"), CoreWeave,[[29]](#cite_note-Nicoletti-29) Cipher Mining, [TeraWulf](/wiki/TeraWulf "TeraWulf"),[[30]](#cite_note-30) IREN, Core Scientific, and CleanSpark[[31]](#cite_note-31) have also been involved with AI data centers.

## Finances

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Private_investment_in_generative_AI_-_2024_AI_index.jpg/250px-Private_investment_in_generative_AI_-_2024_AI_index.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Private_investment_in_generative_AI_-_2024_AI_index.jpg)

Between January and August 2024, Microsoft, Meta, Google and Amazon collectively spent $125 billion on AI data centers.[[32]](#cite_note-32) [Citigroup](/wiki/Citigroup "Citigroup") forecasted that $2.8 trillion would be spent on AI data centers by 2030,[[13]](#cite_note-Booth-13) while [McKinsey and Company](/wiki/McKinsey_and_Company "McKinsey and Company") estimated that almost $7 trillion would be spent globally by that time.[[33]](#cite_note-Kerr-33) According to [S&P Global](/wiki/S%26P_Global "S&P Global"), $61 billion has been spent on the data center market as a whole in 2025, while debt issuance for data centers was $182 billion during the same year.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

Large technology companies have offloaded the financial risks of building AI data centers by setting up [special purpose vehicles](/wiki/Special-purpose_entity "Special-purpose entity") or by contracting with neoclouds. For example, Meta's Hyperion was mostly funded by [Blue Owl Capital](/wiki/Blue_Owl_Capital "Blue Owl Capital"), which did so using a bond offering from [PIMCO](/wiki/PIMCO "PIMCO"). Those bonds were sold to a number of clients, including [BlackRock](/wiki/BlackRock "BlackRock"). Meta did not borrow money itself and instead established a special purpose vehicle from which it would rent the data center.[[18]](#cite_note-Weise-18) This deal was structured by [Morgan Stanley](/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") for $30 billion, the largest known private capital transaction as of 2025.[[29]](#cite_note-Nicoletti-29)

Neoclouds such as CoreWeave have gone into debt to buy computer chips from Nvidia for their data centers, and the chips themselves have been used for loan collateral. As of December 2025, CoreWeave took out three GPU-backed loans, collectively worth $12.4 billion, from private credit firms ([Blackstone](/wiki/Blackstone_Inc. "Blackstone Inc."), [Coatue](/wiki/Coatue_Management "Coatue Management"), [BlackRock](/wiki/BlackRock "BlackRock"), [PIMCO](/wiki/PIMCO "PIMCO")) and from banks ([Goldman Sachs](/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs"), [JPMorgan Chase](/wiki/JPMorgan_Chase "JPMorgan Chase"), [Wells Fargo](/wiki/Wells_Fargo "Wells Fargo")). ## Energy sourcing

This section is an excerpt from [Data center § Energy use and environmental impact](/wiki/Data_center#Energy_use_and_environmental_impact "Data center").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Data_center&action=edit)]

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/2015-_Data_center_power_demand_-_US.svg/250px-2015-_Data_center_power_demand_-_US.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:2015-_Data_center_power_demand_-_US.svg)

Fueled by growth in artificial intelligence, data centers' demand for power increased in the 2020s.[[36]](#cite_note-Data_center_WashPost_20251225-36)

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Google_Data_Center%2C_The_Dalles.jpg/250px-Google_Data_Center%2C_The_Dalles.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Google_Data_Center,_The_Dalles.jpg)

[Google Data Center](/wiki/Google_Data_Centers "Google Data Centers"), [The Dalles, Oregon](/wiki/The_Dalles,_Oregon "The Dalles, Oregon")

Energy consumption and the environmental impacts it creates are a central issue for data centers.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38) Power draw ranges from a few kilowatts (kW) for small server racks to several tens of megawatts (MW) for large facilities. Modern hyperscale data centers can exhibit power densities exceeding 100 times those of conventional office buildings, primarily due to the high concentration of servers and cooling systems required to manage continuous digital workloads.[[39]](#cite_note-39) For higher power density facilities, electricity costs are a dominant [operating expense](/wiki/Operating_expense "Operating expense") and account for over 10% of the [total cost of ownership](/wiki/Total_cost_of_ownership "Total cost of ownership") (TCO) of a data center.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

title: AI data center
text:
Energy consumption and the environmental impacts it creates are a central issue for data centers.[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38) Power draw ranges from a few kilowatts (kW) for small server racks to several tens of megawatts (MW) for large facilities. Modern hyperscale data centers can exhibit power densities exceeding 100 times those of conventional office buildings, primarily due to the high concentration of servers and cooling systems required to manage continuous digital workloads.[[39]](#cite_note-39) For higher power density facilities, electricity costs are a dominant [operating expense](/wiki/Operating_expense "Operating expense") and account for over 10% of the [total cost of ownership](/wiki/Total_cost_of_ownership "Total cost of ownership") (TCO) of a data center.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

As of 2024, data centers in the U.S. are primarily powered by natural gas, which supplies 40% of their electricity (with [renewable energy](/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") at 24%, nuclear at about 20%, and coal at about 15%).[[41]](#cite_note-Data_center_:03-41) The *[Associated Press](/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press")* reported that electricity for AI data centers in the U.S. would likely come from natural gas or oil, as companies prefer using currently available power plants, which primarily use fossil fuels. Fossil energy is also often cheaper in locations where data centers are developed, and experts believe that energy demands from [generative AI](/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI") and data centers would be difficult to fulfill with renewable energy alone.

title: AI data center
text:
As of 2024, data centers in the U.S. are primarily powered by natural gas, which supplies 40% of their electricity (with [renewable energy](/wiki/Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") at 24%, nuclear at about 20%, and coal at about 15%).[[41]](#cite_note-Data_center_:03-41) The *[Associated Press](/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press")* reported that electricity for AI data centers in the U.S. would likely come from natural gas or oil, as companies prefer using currently available power plants, which primarily use fossil fuels. Fossil energy is also often cheaper in locations where data centers are developed, and experts believe that energy demands from [generative AI](/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI") and data centers would be difficult to fulfill with renewable energy alone.

Some companies such as Google, Amazon, and Meta have expressed interest in [nuclear power](/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") for their data centers.[[42]](#cite_note-Data_center_:7-42) As of 2020, according to the [IEA](/wiki/International_Energy_Agency "International Energy Agency"), solar [photovoltaic](/wiki/Photovoltaics "Photovoltaics")-generated electricity is at its lowest cost in history.[[43]](#cite_note-43) Other data centers, including xAI's [Colossus](/wiki/Colossus_(supercomputer) "Colossus (supercomputer)"), OpenAI's [Stargate](/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC"), and Meta's Prometheus use their own off-grid [natural gas plants](/wiki/Gas-fired_power_plant "Gas-fired power plant").[[44]](#cite_note-Data_center_:32-44)[[45]](#cite_note-Data_center_:8-45) [Electric vehicle](/wiki/Electric_vehicle_battery "Electric vehicle battery") and [lithium-ion batteries](/wiki/Lithium-ion_battery "Lithium-ion battery") have also been used for powering data centers, including for Colossus.[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-Data_center_:21-47)

[Power utility](/wiki/Electric_utility "Electric utility") companies make upgrades to their infrastructure to handle demands of new data centers, and the price for these changes typically falls on residential or smaller commercial consumers.[[41]](#cite_note-Data_center_:03-41)[[42]](#cite_note-Data_center_:7-42)[[48]](#cite_note-Data_center_:10-48) In 2025, the [Mountain Valley Pipeline](/wiki/Mountain_Valley_Pipeline "Mountain Valley Pipeline") announced plans to expand its capacity by 25% to meet energy needs for data centers.[[49]](#cite_note-Data_center_:6-49)

In December 2025, the [Federal Energy Regulatory Commission](/wiki/Federal_Energy_Regulatory_Commission "Federal Energy Regulatory Commission") (FERC) published a unanimous order allowing data centers in the U.S. to have a direct connection with [power plants](/wiki/Power_plants "Power plants").[[50]](#cite_note-50) United States Secretary of Energy [Chris Wright](/wiki/Chris_Wright "Chris Wright") expressed support for un-retiring coal plants to power AI data centers.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Electricity demands from AI data centers have slowed or reversed the retirement of [peaking power plants](/wiki/Peaking_power_plant "Peaking power plant") in the U.S.[[52]](#cite_note-Data_center_:22-52) For example, in 2025, [Southern Company](/wiki/Southern_Company "Southern Company") announced that energy use from data centers would prevent the company from retiring coal-fired power plants as it had earlier promised.[[49]](#cite_note-Data_center_:6-49) In [Nevada](/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), the [Desert Research Institute](/wiki/Desert_Research_Institute "Desert Research Institute") (DRI) calculated that 35% of the state's energy production could go to data centers by the year 2030 if all projects planned in the state as of 2026 are completed.[[53]](#cite_note-Data_center_:15-53) DRI also stated, in areas where there are clusters of data centers, local consumers may end up paying the extra cost of expanding infrastructure.[[53]](#cite_note-Data_center_:15-53)

title: AI data center
text:
## Environmental footprint

See also: [Environmental impact of artificial intelligence](/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_artificial_intelligence "Environmental impact of artificial intelligence")

Average AI data centers have an electricity footprint equivalent to 100,000 households, and use billions of gallons of water for cooling their hardware.[[54]](#cite_note-54) In 2025, the [International Energy Agency](/wiki/International_Energy_Agency "International Energy Agency") estimated that the larger AI data centers currently under construction could consume as much electricity as 2 million households.[[9]](#cite_note-Leppert-9) A 2024 report from the [United States Department of Energy](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") stated that data centers overall used 17 billion gallons of water per year in the United States, primarily due to "rapid proliferation of AI servers", and that this usage was forecasted to grow to nearly 80 billion gallons by 2028.[[33]](#cite_note-Kerr-33) Researchers estimated that AI data centers in the United States would emit 24–44 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and use 731–1,125 million cubic meters of water per year between 2024 and 2030.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

Peaking power plants, which have been proposed as a power source for AI data centers, emit [sulfur dioxide](/wiki/Sulfur_dioxide "Sulfur dioxide") and have historically been located disproportionately near communities of color in the United States.[[56]](#cite_note-56)

Reciprocating internal combustion engines, proposed as another power source for a data center, emit [PM 2.5](/wiki/Particulate_matter "Particulate matter"), [nitrogen oxides](/wiki/Nitrogen_oxides "Nitrogen oxides"), and [volatile organic compounds](/wiki/Volatile_organic_compound "Volatile organic compound").[[57]](#cite_note-57)

## Global memory supply shortage

Main article: [2024–2026 global memory supply shortage](/wiki/2024%E2%80%932026_global_memory_supply_shortage "2024–2026 global memory supply shortage")

The construction of AI data centers during the AI boom starting in 2024 has exhausted the global supply of the computer memory. To meet demand from AI servers, the three major DRAM manufacturers, [Samsung](/wiki/Samsung "Samsung"), [SK Hynix](/wiki/SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"), and [Micron](/wiki/Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), prioritized production of [High Bandwidth Memory](/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory "High Bandwidth Memory") (HBM) and high-end server DRAM, contributing to a global memory supply shortage and intensifying competition for advanced memory chips.[[3]](#cite_note-reuters-ai-frenzy-3) Because HBM consumes far more fabrication capacity than conventional memory—producing a single bit of HBM requires roughly three times the wafer capacity of DDR5.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

The resulting price increases and shortages have affected computer memory broadly, including HBM, [DRAM](/wiki/Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), and [NAND flash memory](/wiki/NAND_flash_memory "NAND flash memory").[[3]](#cite_note-reuters-ai-frenzy-3)[[59]](#cite_note-59)[[60]](#cite_note-60)

Under an agreement with Samsung and SK Hynix, the [Stargate](/wiki/Stargate_LLC "Stargate LLC") project alone is set to receive 900,000 DRAM wafers per month, roughly 40% of total global DRAM production.[[61]](#cite_note-61)

title: AI data center
text:
## In the United States

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Data_center_infrastructure_in_the_United_States.jpg/250px-Data_center_infrastructure_in_the_United_States.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Data_center_infrastructure_in_the_United_States.jpg)

Data center infrastructure in the United States (2025)

In the United States, both the [Biden administration](/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden "Presidency of Joe Biden") and [second Trump administration](/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump") supported the construction of AI data centers. In January 2025, then-president Joe Biden signed an executive order for federal government agencies to support AI data centers on federal sites built by private companies, study their effect on energy prices, and encourage their use of renewable energy.[[62]](#cite_note-62) In April 2025, the [United States Department of Energy](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy") suggested 16 possible sites, including [Los Alamos National Laboratory](/wiki/Los_Alamos_National_Laboratory "Los Alamos National Laboratory"), [Sandia National Laboratories](/wiki/Sandia_National_Laboratories "Sandia National Laboratories") and [Oak Ridge National Laboratory](/wiki/Oak_Ridge_National_Laboratory "Oak Ridge National Laboratory").[[63]](#cite_note-63) In its July 2025 AI Action Plan, the second Trump administration supported increased production of AI data centers.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

Several US states have incentivized local data center construction.[[65]](#cite_note-65) For example, in 2024, lawmakers in Michigan approved tax breaks for data center equipment and construction material.[[66]](#cite_note-Larson-66) Some data center companies have also invested or promised to invest in the infrastructure of local communities.[[67]](#cite_note-Dellinger-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68)

In December 2025, [Democratic](/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") senators [Elizabeth Warren](/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren"), [Chris Van Hollen](/wiki/Chris_Van_Hollen "Chris Van Hollen"), and [Richard Blumenthal](/wiki/Richard_Blumenthal "Richard Blumenthal") wrote to seven technology companies (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, CoreWeave, Digital Realty, and [Equinix](/wiki/Equinix "Equinix")) that they will investigate the effects of those companies' operations on consumer energy bills, highlighting AI data centers in particular.[[69]](#cite_note-69) That same month, 25 Democratic lawmakers wrote to the inspector general of the [United States Department of Commerce](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce") over possible [conflict of interest](/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest") concerns involving secretary of commerce [Howard Lutnick](/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick") and AI data centers. Lutnick met with a co-founder of Fermi, which proposed an AI data center project financed by [Cantor Fitzgerald](/wiki/Cantor_Fitzgerald "Cantor Fitzgerald") and [Newmark Group](/wiki/Newmark_Group "Newmark Group").[[70]](#cite_note-70)

AI Infrastructure Coalition (AIIC), an organization led by Brian O. Walsh, [Kyrsten Sinema](/wiki/Kyrsten_Sinema "Kyrsten Sinema"), and [Garret Graves](/wiki/Garret_Graves "Garret Graves"), has supported Trump's AI Action Plan,[[71]](#cite_note-Allen-71) with Sinema becoming personally involved in a local meeting on an AI data center in Arizona.[[72]](#cite_note-Plautz-72) Venture capital firm [Andreessen Horowitz](/wiki/Andreessen_Horowitz "Andreessen Horowitz"), Big Tech companies (Google, Meta, Microsoft), telecommunications companies ([Cisco](/wiki/Cisco "Cisco"), [Corning Inc.](/wiki/Corning_Inc. "Corning Inc."), [Lumen Technologies](/wiki/Lumen_Technologies "Lumen Technologies")), data center providers (Digital Realty, QTS), energy companies ([Duke Energy](/wiki/Duke_Energy "Duke Energy"), [Entergy](/wiki/Entergy "Entergy"), ExxonMobil, NextEra Energy), and utility companies ([PG&E](/wiki/Pacific_Gas_and_Electric_Company "Pacific Gas and Electric Company"), [Pinnacle West Capital](/wiki/Pinnacle_West_Capital "Pinnacle West Capital")) are members of AIIC as of November 2025.[[71]](#cite_note-Allen-71) AIIC has been supported by [Hogan Lovells](/wiki/Hogan_Lovells "Hogan Lovells").[[72]](#cite_note-Plautz-72)

According to [Goldman Sachs](/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") in 2025 an addition half million workers will be needed by 2030 to build the power infrastructure, which is acute because of AI data center build out.[[73]](#cite_note-73)[[74]](#cite_note-74)[[75]](#cite_note-75)

title: AI data center
text:
### Concerns and opposition

Main article: [Opposition to AI data centers](/wiki/Opposition_to_AI_data_centers "Opposition to AI data centers")

Some analysts have expressed concerns about overbuilding of AI data centers, warning that their infrastructure risks [obsolescence](/wiki/Technological_obsolescence "Technological obsolescence") due to changes in demand and technology.[[26]](#cite_note-Berg-26) Estimates for the lifespan of the GPUs used to power data centers range from one to eight years.[[76]](#cite_note-76)[[77]](#cite_note-77) By contrast, CPUs in more traditional data centers have a shelf life of about 5–7 years. Machine learning model training causes significant stress on computer chips.[[78]](#cite_note-78)

Advocates have also linked data center construction to the [AI bubble](/wiki/AI_bubble "AI bubble").[[79]](#cite_note-79)[[80]](#cite_note-80) [Wisconsin Watch](/wiki/Wisconsin_Center_for_Investigative_Journalism "Wisconsin Center for Investigative Journalism") expressed concern that data centers could become [stranded assets](/wiki/Stranded_assets "Stranded assets") in the context of an AI bubble, leaving energy customers to pay for the costs.[[81]](#cite_note-81) Journalists have warned that the large number of links between actors and organizations in the AI ecosystem[[17]](#cite_note-Lopatto-17) as well as the large number of companies involved[[29]](#cite_note-Nicoletti-29) each indicate strong risks for the [global economy](/wiki/World_economy "World economy") and [financial markets](/wiki/Financial_market "Financial market").

A hedge fund founder questioned the economics of AI data centers, concluding that they need about $1 trillion of revenue for profitability.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

A hedge fund founder questioned the economics of AI data centers, concluding that they need about $1 trillion of revenue for profitability.[[82]](#cite_note-82)

In November 2025, the [North American Electric Reliability Corporation](/wiki/North_American_Electric_Reliability_Corporation "North American Electric Reliability Corporation") warned that building new data centers could negatively affect the [electrical grid](/wiki/Electrical_grid "Electrical grid") and cause power outages during [extreme weather](/wiki/Extreme_weather "Extreme weather").[[83]](#cite_note-FT-83) The independent monitor of [PJM Interconnection](/wiki/PJM_Interconnection "PJM Interconnection") warned that its [power grid](/wiki/Electrical_grid "Electrical grid") cannot support new data centers and supported a federal moratorium on data centers.[[24]](#cite_note-Halper-24)

In November 2025, the [North American Electric Reliability Corporation](/wiki/North_American_Electric_Reliability_Corporation "North American Electric Reliability Corporation") warned that building new data centers could negatively affect the [electrical grid](/wiki/Electrical_grid "Electrical grid") and cause power outages during [extreme weather](/wiki/Extreme_weather "Extreme weather").[[83]](#cite_note-FT-83) The independent monitor of [PJM Interconnection](/wiki/PJM_Interconnection "PJM Interconnection") warned that its [power grid](/wiki/Electrical_grid "Electrical grid") cannot support new data centers and supported a federal moratorium on data centers.[[24]](#cite_note-Halper-24)

Machine learning developers, when [training](/wiki/Model_training "Model training") [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model"), often use data centers at their full capacity, conflicting with other users (including households) during peak usage, which may lead to [blackouts](/wiki/Power_outage "Power outage").[[83]](#cite_note-FT-83)

Power disruptions in data centers can cause errors in machine learning model calculations ("silent data corruption").[[84]](#cite_note-84)

Machine learning developers, when [training](/wiki/Model_training "Model training") [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model"), often use data centers at their full capacity, conflicting with other users (including households) during peak usage, which may lead to [blackouts](/wiki/Power_outage "Power outage").[[83]](#cite_note-FT-83)

Power disruptions in data centers can cause errors in machine learning model calculations ("silent data corruption").[[84]](#cite_note-84)

Large technology companies who are building data centers have asked public officials and land owners to sign [non-disclosure agreements](/wiki/Non-disclosure_agreement "Non-disclosure agreement") and have appeared to use [shell companies](/wiki/Shell_corporation "Shell corporation").[[85]](#cite_note-85) In one case, when a joint OpenAI-Oracle data center was rejected by [Saline Township](/wiki/Saline_Township,_Michigan "Saline Township, Michigan") in Michigan, landowners and developers responded by suing the town.[[66]](#cite_note-Larson-66)[[86]](#cite_note-86) The developers acquired the land from the resulting settlement. The [Michigan Public Service Commission](/wiki/Michigan_Public_Service_Commission "Michigan Public Service Commission") approved [DTE Energy](/wiki/DTE_Energy "DTE Energy") to provide power to the data center, part of Stargate. The approval was part of an [ex parte](/wiki/Ex_parte "Ex parte") motion, with no public input.[[67]](#cite_note-Dellinger-67)

In 2025, over 230 groups have signed a letter supporting a moratorium on constructing AI data centers in the United States, concerned by impact on the environment and energy bills. Signatories include [Food & Water Watch](/wiki/Food_%26_Water_Watch "Food & Water Watch"), [Greenpeace](/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace"), [Friends of the Earth](/wiki/Friends_of_the_Earth "Friends of the Earth") and [Physicians for Social Responsibility](/wiki/Physicians_for_Social_Responsibility "Physicians for Social Responsibility").[[87]](#cite_note-87) Senator [Bernie Sanders](/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") has also supported a moratorium on AI data centers.[[88]](#cite_note-88)

Ashley LaMont, of [Honor the Earth](/wiki/Honor_the_Earth "Honor the Earth"), argued that data centers on tribal lands would not help Native Americans obtain [data sovereignty](/wiki/Data_sovereignty "Data sovereignty").[[89]](#cite_note-89)

The [NAACP](/wiki/NAACP "NAACP") has also expressed opposition to AI data centers.[[90]](#cite_note-90)

title: AI data center
text:
## In space

See also: [Space-based data center](/wiki/Space-based_data_center "Space-based data center")

Several tech companies, including [Starcloud](/wiki/Starcloud "Starcloud"), Google, Nvidia, [Blue Origin](/wiki/Blue_Origin "Blue Origin") and [SpaceX](/wiki/SpaceX "SpaceX"), have announced projects for or otherwise expressed interest in building data centers in outer space.[[91]](#cite_note-91)[[92]](#cite_note-92)[[93]](#cite_note-93)[[94]](#cite_note-94) Google announced Project Suncatcher, which plans to test whether its [Tensor Processing Unit](/wiki/Tensor_Processing_Unit "Tensor Processing Unit") (TPU) chips (which are specifically designed for machine learning) can function in the environment of space. The company aims to deploy satellites with these chips in a data center by 2027.[[95]](#cite_note-95) In November 2025, Starcloud, a startup supported by Nvidia, launched a satellite with an [Nvidia H100 GPU](/wiki/Hopper_(microarchitecture) "Hopper (microarchitecture)") that the company used to deploy and develop a large language model. [CNBC](/wiki/CNBC "CNBC") reported that this model, NanoGPT, was the first model trained in space. Starcloud deployed a second model based on Google's [Gemma](/wiki/Gemma_(language_model) "Gemma (language model)").[[96]](#cite_note-96)

title: AI observability
text:
[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Ai_observability_diagram.png/500px-Ai_observability_diagram.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Ai_observability_diagram.png)

Telemetry is collected from three layers of an AI system (infrastructure, model, and output) and aggregated by the observability layer.

**AI observability** is the practice of collecting and analyzing [telemetry](/wiki/Telemetry "Telemetry"), data such as [logs](/wiki/Log_file "Log file"), metrics, and [traces](/wiki/Tracing_(software) "Tracing (software)") that a system automatically records as it runs, from [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") systems deployed in production, in order to understand how they behave and how well they perform in terms of accuracy, cost, and safety. It applies the idea of [observability](/wiki/Observability "Observability"), which comes from [control theory](/wiki/Control_theory "Control theory") and [software engineering](/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering"), to systems based on [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") models, and in particular to [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") (LLMs) and [autonomous agents](/wiki/Software_agent "Software agent"). In control theory, observability is a measure of how well the internal state of a system can be inferred from its external outputs.[[1]](#cite_note-kalman-1)

title: AI observability
text:
**AI observability** is the practice of collecting and analyzing [telemetry](/wiki/Telemetry "Telemetry"), data such as [logs](/wiki/Log_file "Log file"), metrics, and [traces](/wiki/Tracing_(software) "Tracing (software)") that a system automatically records as it runs, from [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") systems deployed in production, in order to understand how they behave and how well they perform in terms of accuracy, cost, and safety. It applies the idea of [observability](/wiki/Observability "Observability"), which comes from [control theory](/wiki/Control_theory "Control theory") and [software engineering](/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering"), to systems based on [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") models, and in particular to [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") (LLMs) and [autonomous agents](/wiki/Software_agent "Software agent"). In control theory, observability is a measure of how well the internal state of a system can be inferred from its external outputs.[[1]](#cite_note-kalman-1)

AI observability is often distinguished from conventional monitoring. Where monitoring relies on predefined metrics, thresholds, and alerts to signal that a problem has occurred, observability aims to provide enough context to understand why it occurred. The distinction matters for AI systems in particular, because a system can appear healthy by standard infrastructure measures, such as latency or error rate, while still producing answers that are wrong, irrelevant, or unsafe.[[2]](#cite_note-majors2022-2)

title: AI observability
text:
AI observability is often distinguished from conventional monitoring. Where monitoring relies on predefined metrics, thresholds, and alerts to signal that a problem has occurred, observability aims to provide enough context to understand why it occurred. The distinction matters for AI systems in particular, because a system can appear healthy by standard infrastructure measures, such as latency or error rate, while still producing answers that are wrong, irrelevant, or unsafe.[[2]](#cite_note-majors2022-2)

One of the signals that AI observability tracks is the change in a model's behavior over time, a phenomenon studied in machine learning under the name of [concept drift](/wiki/Concept_drift "Concept drift").[[3]](#cite_note-lu2019-3) AI observability is closely related to [MLOps](/wiki/MLOps "MLOps") (machine learning operations), and it is sometimes treated as one of its parts. When it is applied specifically to language models or to agent-based systems, it is also called *LLM observability* or *agent observability*.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

title: AI observability
text:
## Background

The term *observability* originates in [control theory](/wiki/Control_theory "Control theory"), where it was introduced by [Rudolf E. Kálmán](/wiki/Rudolf_E._K%C3%A1lm%C3%A1n "Rudolf E. Kálmán") in 1960 to describe how well the internal states of a [dynamical system](/wiki/Dynamical_system "Dynamical system") can be inferred from measurements of its outputs. In software engineering, the term became popular from the mid-2010s to describe the ability to understand the internal state of complex [distributed systems](/wiki/Distributed_system "Distributed system") from the telemetry they produce, commonly organized into the "three pillars" of [logs](/wiki/Log_file "Log file"), metrics, and [traces](/wiki/Tracing_(software) "Tracing (software)").[[5]](#cite_note-sridharan2018-5)

Applying observability to AI systems raises challenges that do not arise in conventional software. In traditional systems, identical inputs and states are expected to produce identical outputs, and faults can typically be traced to specific code sections. Machine learning models sample from probability distributions instead, so a system may show normal operational characteristics while still generating undesirable outputs such as [hallucinations](/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence) "Hallucination (artificial intelligence)").[[6]](#cite_note-huang2025-6) That gap motivated adding behavioral and semantic telemetry, covering prompt and response content, output quality, and model [drift](/wiki/Concept_drift "Concept drift"), alongside the conventional signals of software monitoring.[[2]](#cite_note-majors2022-2)

title: AI observability
text:
## Observability versus monitoring

Although the two terms are sometimes used as synonyms, the literature usually keeps them separate.[[7]](#cite_note-zhou2021-7) Monitoring is defined as the collection of predefined measurements against known thresholds, producing alerts when those thresholds are crossed; it addresses questions that operators already know to ask. Observability is the broader capability, allowing operators to investigate unanticipated behavior by correlating diverse signals across the system rather than responding only to known alert conditions. A monitoring-only approach therefore depends on experienced engineers knowing in advance what to look for, while observability supports open-ended investigation of any anomaly.[[2]](#cite_note-majors2022-2)

In the context of AI systems, this distinction is often framed in terms of an additional, behavioral dimension layered on the conventional pillars of telemetry. Infrastructure-level signals may indicate that a model is responding quickly and without errors, while separate signals are required to assess whether its outputs are accurate, relevant, compliant with policy, and free of unsafe content.[[2]](#cite_note-majors2022-2)

title: AI observability
text:
## Signals and dimensions

AI observability builds on the standard telemetry signals of software engineering, namely logs, metrics, and traces, and adds dimensions specific to machine learning models. The dimensions that are most often described are:[[5]](#cite_note-sridharan2018-5)[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

- Inputs and outputs: the prompts sent to a model and the responses it returns. These are sometimes stored in full so that problems can be studied later.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)
- Cost and resource usage: how many tokens a request uses and how much it costs, together with latency. These are common measures of inference efficiency and help identify waste and unexpected expense.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)
- Performance: latency, throughput, and error rate, as in traditional [application performance management](/wiki/Application_performance_management "Application performance management").[[7]](#cite_note-zhou2021-7)
- Output quality: how relevant, accurate, and well aligned with the prompt the answer is. These properties usually cannot be checked by normal code, and they include the rate of [hallucinations](/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence) "Hallucination (artificial intelligence)").[[6]](#cite_note-huang2025-6)
- Behavior over time: changes in the model, known as [drift](/wiki/Concept_drift "Concept drift"), and worse results after a model or prompt change.[[3]](#cite_note-lu2019-3)[[8]](#cite_note-hinder2024-8)
- Safety and policy: finding policy violations, unsafe content, and unusual usage.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

- Cost and resource usage: how many tokens a request uses and how much it costs, together with latency. These are common measures of inference efficiency and help identify waste and unexpected expense.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)
- Performance: latency, throughput, and error rate, as in traditional [application performance management](/wiki/Application_performance_management "Application performance management").[[7]](#cite_note-zhou2021-7)
- Output quality: how relevant, accurate, and well aligned with the prompt the answer is. These properties usually cannot be checked by normal code, and they include the rate of [hallucinations](/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence) "Hallucination (artificial intelligence)").[[6]](#cite_note-huang2025-6)
- Behavior over time: changes in the model, known as [drift](/wiki/Concept_drift "Concept drift"), and worse results after a model or prompt change.[[3]](#cite_note-lu2019-3)[[8]](#cite_note-hinder2024-8)
- Safety and policy: finding policy violations, unsafe content, and unusual usage.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

For [agent](/wiki/Software_agent "Software agent")-based systems, more signals are needed because the work happens in many steps. These signals record the intermediate reasoning steps, the calls to external tools and [APIs](/wiki/Application_programming_interface "Application programming interface"), and the [retrieval-augmented generation](/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation "Retrieval-augmented generation") chains.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

title: AI observability
text:
## Techniques and methods

Techniques associated with AI observability include:[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

- End to end [tracing](/wiki/Tracing_(software) "Tracing (software)") of requests as they move through pipelines, chains, or agent steps, so that each stage of the execution becomes visible.[[9]](#cite_note-otel-genai-9)
- Structured [logging](/wiki/Logging_(software) "Logging (software)") of events, including model identifiers, timestamps, and request and response pairs.[[9]](#cite_note-otel-genai-9)
- [Anomaly detection](/wiki/Anomaly_detection "Anomaly detection") over the telemetry, in order to surface unexpected behavior.[[8]](#cite_note-hinder2024-8)
- Synthetic monitoring, in which predefined test prompts are sent repeatedly, for example after a model or prompt update, to detect regressions.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)
- Automated evaluation, including the use of one language model to assess the output of another, an approach often called "LLM-as-a-judge"[[10]](#cite_note-llm-as-a-judge-survey-10), for qualities that are difficult to measure with conventional code.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)
- [Human-in-the-loop](/wiki/Human-in-the-loop "Human-in-the-loop") review at important checkpoints.[[4]](#cite_note-mohammadi2025-4)

title: AI observability
text:
### Open source tools and standards

Because AI observability is a new field, several open standards and open source tools have been created to avoid tying telemetry to a single vendor. The most notable effort is the set of semantic conventions for generative AI defined by [OpenTelemetry](/wiki/OpenTelemetry "OpenTelemetry"), a [Cloud Native Computing Foundation](/wiki/Cloud_Native_Computing_Foundation "Cloud Native Computing Foundation") project. These conventions describe a common way to record model calls, token usage, tool and agent calls, and evaluation scores, so that telemetry produced by one tool can be read by another.[[9]](#cite_note-otel-genai-9) As of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=AI_observability&action=edit), these conventions are still under active development and are not yet marked as stable.[[9]](#cite_note-otel-genai-9)

Open source instrumentation libraries can generate telemetry that follows these conventions automatically for common model providers and frameworks. Separately, several open source projects focus on tracing and evaluating machine learning and LLM applications, and some of them can export or import data in the OpenTelemetry format, which allows them to work together with general purpose observability backends instead of only their own dashboard.[[11]](#cite_note-mlflow-otel-11)
